name: Lelantine Plain
place: Lelantine plain between Chalcis and Eretria, Euboea
sources: Plut. Amat. 17 (760e–761b, citing Aristotle); cf. Thuc. 1.15.3; Hdt. 5.99; Strabo 10.1.12
note: Cavalry battle won by Thessalian (Pharsalian) horse hired by Chalcis; known only from Plutarch. Most scholars accept the war as historical, but its date and the details of this battle are uncertain.

name: Hysiae
place: Hysiae, on the Argos–Tegea road, Argolid (near mod. Achladokampos)
note: Pausanias is the only source; he dates it to Ol. 27.4, in the Athenian archonship of Peisistratus. It is often linked to Pheidon of Argos, but that is speculative, and a few scholars doubt the battle happened.

name: Smyrna
place: Smyrna and the Hermus plain, Ionia
sources: Paus. 4.21.5, 9.29.4; Mimnermus fr. 13–14 W; cf. Hdt. 1.14
note: Pausanias says the Smyrnaeans drove Gyges and the Lydians out after the Lydians had occupied the town, and that Mimnermus wrote elegies on the battle. Mimnermus fr. 14 describes a fight against Lydian cavalry in the Hermus plain. Exact site and date unknown.

name: Corcyra
place: probably in Corcyraean waters, Ionian Sea (site unrecorded)
note: Thucydides calls it the oldest sea battle known, c. 260 years before the end of 'this war' (664 if reckoned from 404, 681 if from 421). He does not name the winner, so the outcome is entered as 'unknown'. Sides are listed alphabetically, not by victor.

name: Great Foss
note: The only Second Messenian War battle kept here. The Arcadian king Aristocrates' betrayal is attested independently by Callisthenes, who reports an inscription at the altar of Zeus Lykaios. The narrative in Pausanias comes from the Hellenistic Aristomenes romance (Rhianus), and the date and site are uncertain. Deres and Boar's Grave are excluded as legendary.

name: Limeneion
note: One of the two great Milesian defeats in the war, which ran six years under Sadyattes and five under Alyattes. Absolute dates depend on Lydian chronology. Chios was Miletus' only ally.

name: Maeander plain
place: plain of the Maeander, near Miletus
note: The second of the two great Milesian defeats. Its date relative to Limeneion is unknown.

name: Sigeion
place: Sigeion, at the mouth of the Hellespont, Troad
sources: Hdt. 5.94–95; Strabo 13.1.38; Diog. Laert. 1.74; Alcaeus fr. 428
note: Herodotus says the Athenians had the better of the fighting and that Alcaeus fled, leaving his arms as a trophy. In the same war Pittacus killed Phrynon in single combat (Eusebius dates the duel 607/6). The war was ended by Periander's arbitration, which gave Sigeion to Athens.

name: Massalia (sea)
place: off Massalia, Gulf of Lion (site unrecorded)
note: Thucydides says the Phocaeans beat the Carthaginians at sea while founding Massalia. Later sources mention repeated Massaliot victories. The site is unknown.

name: Salamis
place: island of Salamis, near the old town
note: This follows Plutarch's alternative version (Sol. 9): Solon landed with 500 volunteers and beat the Megarians in a land battle while a captured ship took the town. The popular version (Sol. 8) is an ambush at Cape Colias. The tradition is anecdotal, and Megara later recovered the island.

name: Clazomenae
note: Alyattes attacked Clazomenae after taking Smyrna and 'suffered a great reverse'. Herodotus gives no details of the battle.

name: Perinthus
note: A Samian relief force of 30 ships beat the Megarians attacking Samos' colony Perinthus and captured 600. Plutarch does not say whether the fight was on land or at sea, and the date is approximate. The generals then used the prisoners to overthrow the Samian Geomori. Obscure; included with reservation.

name: Lilybaeum
note: Pentathlus' colonists fought for Selinus against Segesta and were defeated, and Pentathlus was killed. The survivors founded Lipara. Pausanias (from Antiochus) names Elymians and Phoenicians as the victors and puts the colonists at Cape Pachynum, probably an error.

name: Ceressus
place: Ceressus, a stronghold in Thespian territory near Leuctra, Boeotia
sources: Plut. Cam. 19.4; Plut. De Herod. Malig. 33 (866e–f); Paus. 9.14.2
note: The Boeotians beat the Thessalians. Plutarch's Camillus puts it more than 200 years before Leuctra (so before 571), but De Herod. Malig. says it came shortly before 480, and modern dates range from the early 6th c. to the 480s. Ceressus itself is unidentified.

name: Irasa
place: Irasa, at the spring Thestes, west of Derna (area of Ain Mara)
note: Apries sent an Egyptian army at the request of the Libyan king Adicran, and it was destroyed. The disaster set off the revolt that made Amasis pharaoh. Also called the Battle of the Well of Thestis.

name: Fetters (Tegea)
note: The 'Battle of the Fetters'. The Spartans brought chains for the Tegeans and were defeated, and the prisoners were made to work the Tegean plain in those chains. Herodotus implies the reign of Leon and Agasicles, while Pausanias puts it under Charillus. Sparta's later supremacy over Tegea (Hdt. 1.67–68, c. 550) is not described as a single battle and is excluded.

name: Priene
date: mid-6th c. BCE (seven years before Drys; time of Bias)
note: A 'great battle' in which the Prienians killed 1,000 Samians. Plutarch, probably drawing on Aristotle, gives no site or date; the date is inferred from the link to Bias. Obscure.

name: Leucon
place: Leucon, in Libya east of Cyrene (site unidentified)
note: Arcesilaus II pursued Libyans whom his estranged brothers, the founders of Barca, had stirred up. At Leucon the Libyans turned and killed 7,000 Cyrenaean hoplites. The location is unknown.

name: Drys (the Oak)
note: Seven years after their victory over Samos, the Prienians met the Milesians at 'the Oak' and lost their foremost citizens, the origin of the Prienian oath 'by the darkness at the Oak'. Bias' embassy to Samos is placed at this time. Very obscure; the date is approximate.

name: Sagra
place: river Sagra between Locri and Caulonia (Torbido or Allaro), Calabria
sources: Strabo 6.1.10; Justin 20.2–3; Diod. 8.32; Cic. Nat. D. 2.6
note: A legendary-sized Locrian victory: 10,000 or 15,000 Locrians with Rhegines against 120,000 or 130,000 Crotoniates. The river is unidentified, and most scholars date the battle to the mid-6th c.

name: Thyrea
place: Thyreatis, on the Argive–Laconian border (near mod. Astros)
note: The 'Battle of the 300 Champions'. The fight of 300 picked men a side was disputed, as both claimed victory, and the full battle that followed was won by Sparta, which kept the Thyreatis. It is dated by its link to the fall of Sardis.

name: Pallene
place: near the sanctuary of Athena Pallenis, Attica (mod. Stavros/Gerakas)
note: Peisistratus came from Eretria via Marathon with Argive mercenaries, Theban money and Lygdamis of Naxos, and routed the city army while it was resting after a meal.

name: Alalia
place: Sardinian Sea, off Alalia (Aléria), eastern Corsica
note: Herodotus calls it a 'Cadmean victory': 60 Phocaean ships beat 120 Carthaginian and Etruscan (Caeretan) ships, but 40 were lost and the rest disabled, and the Phocaeans abandoned Alalia for Rhegium and Elea. It was a strategic defeat. The exact site is uncertain.

name: Lipara (sea)
note: Following an oracle to fight with the fewest possible ships, the Liparaeans took four Etruscan squadrons of five ships each and dedicated 20 statues at Delphi. The sources record several such victories but date none of them. The year is a placeholder: after the colony's foundation c. 580 and probably before 480.

name: Miletus (sea)
note: Polycrates beat at sea and captured the Lesbians, who had come in full force to help Miletus, and made the prisoners dig the moat of Samos. 'Lesbians' is entered as Mytilene. The site is unrecorded but presumably near Miletus.

name: Samos (sea)
faction_a: Samian exiles (Polycrates' contingent sent to Cambyses)
note: The Samians Polycrates had sent to serve Cambyses turned back, beat his fleet at sea and landed on Samos. Herodotus reports a variant in which they first went to Egypt and escaped from there.

name: Samos
note: After their naval victory the exiles were beaten on land and went to Sparta. That led to the Spartan–Corinthian siege of Samos (525/4), which is excluded as a siege.

name: Cumae
place: narrow ground between hills and marshes near Cumae, Campania
note: A huge Etruscan coalition, with absurd numbers in the source, was defeated on cramped, marshy ground. The account probably comes from a local Cumaean chronicle.

name: Perinthus
note: After a threefold duel of men, horses and dogs, the Perinthians cried 'paean', fulfilling an oracle, and the Paeonians attacked and routed them. Folkloric; Herodotus says only that it came 'earlier' than Megabazus' attack.

name: Plataea
place: Plataean territory near the Asopus, Boeotia
note: After Corinthian arbitration the Thebans attacked the withdrawing Athenians and were beaten, and Athens fixed the Asopus as the Theban–Plataean border. The date follows Thucydides' 93 years before 427; some emend it to 509.

name: Cydonia
date: c. 519 BCE (sixth year after the settlement)
note: The Samians were the anti-Polycrates exiles who had settled Cydonia, not the Samian state. The Aeginetans with Cretans beat them at sea and enslaved them. Herodotus does not name the Cretan city.

name: Perinthus
note: The Perinthians 'fought bravely for their freedom but were overcome by numbers'. Herodotus does not say whether this was a field battle or a siege, so it is included with reservation.

name: Phaleron
commanders_a: Hippias; Cineas of Conium (1,000 Thessalian cavalry)
note: Athens here means the Peisistratid regime. A Spartan seaborne landing was cut up by Thessalian cavalry on ground the Peisistratids had cleared for horsemen. Anchimolius was buried at Alopeke.

name: Attica
note: Cleomenes' overland army routed the Thessalian cavalry fighting for the Peisistratids, who lost more than 40 men and went home. The siege of the Acropolis that followed is excluded.

name: Crathis
place: between Croton and Sybaris (traditionally the Crathis or Traeis), Calabria
note: Diodorus says 100,000 Crotoniates beat 300,000 Sybarites, both figures inflated; Sybaris was then sacked. The site is not recorded. According to the Sybarites (Hdt. 5.44), Dorieus helped Croton, which the Crotoniates denied.

name: Eryx
note: Dorieus and most of his companions were killed in battle by the Phoenicians and the Segestans while trying to found Heraclea near Eryx. 'Sparta' stands for Dorieus' colonists: Spartans he raised with state sanction, but not a state army.

name: Euripus
war: Athenian war with Boeotia and Chalcis
place: Boeotian shore of the Euripus, opposite Chalcis
note: The Athenians attacked the Boeotians who had come to help Chalcis, killed many and took 700 prisoners. On the same day they crossed and beat the Chalcidians; the double victory was celebrated with a dedication on the Acropolis.

name: Chalcis
war: Athenian war with Boeotia and Chalcis
note: Fought on the same day as the Euripus battle. Afterwards Athens settled 4,000 cleruchs on the land of the Chalcidian Hippobotae.

name: Aricia
note: The Aricians and their Latin allies were routed first, but the Cumaean contingent under Aristodemus attacked the Clusine army from the rear and destroyed it. 'Latins' is a new entity name; the enemy was Clusium.

name: Parnassus (night attack)
note: Tellias of Elis led 600 Phocians, chalked white, in a night attack on the Thessalian camp. Herodotus dates the war 'not many years' before 480; some put it in the mid-6th century.

name: Hyampolis
note: Buried jars broke the legs of the Thessalian horses. Same dating problem as the night attack.

name: Ephesus
place: near Ephesus, Ionia (Greek retreat from Sardis)
note: Persian forces west of the Halys overtook the Greeks returning from the burning of Sardis; Athenians and Eretrians then went home. Athens/Eretria listed as principals because Herodotus treats their contingents as distinct.

name: Salamis in Cyprus
note: Persian victory after the Curian contingent and the Salaminian war-chariots deserted. Fought the same day as the Ionian naval victory off Cyprus.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (sea)
note: Ionian fleet (Samians distinguished) defeated the Phoenician fleet; Persia's side here was the Phoenician navy. The land defeat the same day made the victory useless.

name: Labraunda
place: sanctuary of Zeus Stratios, Labraunda, Caria
note: Second Carian defeat after the Marsyas; the Milesians and their allies came to help and suffered heaviest losses. 'Carians' is a new (non-Greek) entity name; Miletus is the Greek principal.

name: Lade
place: sea off the island of Lade, opposite Miletus (now silted up)
note: 353 Ionian triremes (Chios 100, Miletus 80, Lesbos 70, Samos 60 etc.) v. c. 600 Phoenician, Cypriot, Cilician and Egyptian ships; most Samians and the Lesbians deserted. Former sea now alluvial plain.

name: Sepeia
note: Conventional date 494 (some argue c. 520). Survivors who fled into the grove of Argos were burnt; the battle field itself was a Spartan surprise attack at the midday meal.

name: Malene
note: Histiaeus' army of Ionians and Aeolians, landed from Lesbos to forage, was routed by a Persian cavalry charge. Some date to late 494.

name: Helorus
note: Syracusans routed; Corinth and Corcyra mediated a peace in which Syracuse ceded Camarina.

name: Aegina (sea)
note: Athenian fleet of 70 (incl. 20 ships hired from Corinth), arriving after the failed Nicodromus coup, beat 70 Aeginetan ships. Herodotus places it after Cleomenes' death; many date c. 488–487.

name: Aegina
note: After the sea victory the Athenians landed on Aegina; most of the 1,000 Argive volunteers were killed. Inclusion as a separate battle is a judgement call.

name: Aegina
note: Aeginetans attacked the Athenian fleet while it was in disorder and took four ships with their crews.

name: Artemisium
place: strait off Cape Artemisium, northern Euboea
note: Three days of fighting simultaneous with Thermopylae; indecisive, the Greeks withdrew after news of Thermopylae. Sparta led (Eurybiades) though Athens supplied most ships.

name: Thermopylae
note: Includes the Phocian rout on the Anopaea path. The 700 Thespians died with the Spartans; the Theban 400 surrendered.

name: Salamis
sources: Hdt. 8.40–96; Aesch. Pers. 353–432; Diod. 11.15–19; Plut. Them. 11–15
note: Includes Aristides' hoplite landing on Psyttaleia. Sparta held the command, Athens provided c. 180 of c. 370 ships, Aegina won the prize for valour. Ionian and other Greek subjects fought on the Persian side.

name: Himera
note: Tradition put it on the same day as Salamis (Hdt.) or Thermopylae (Diod.). Carthaginian camp and beached fleet burned.

name: Plataea
note: Includes the preliminary cavalry fight near Erythrae (death of Masistius) and the storming of the Persian camp. Spartans and Tegeans beat the Persians, Athenians beat the Boeotians.

name: Mycale
note: Greek fleet landed and stormed the Persian camp and beached fleet; Samians and Milesians changed sides during the battle.

name: Eion
place: before Eion at the mouth of the Strymon, Thrace
note: Mainly a siege; included only because Plutarch says Cimon first defeated the Persians in battle and shut them in the town. Uncertain whether standard lists count it as a battle.

name: Cumae
sources: Diod. 11.51; Pind. Pyth. 1.71–75; Syll.³ 35 (Hieron's helmets at Olympia)

name: Kailia
note: Sources say 'Iapygians' (Messapians used as canonical name). Hdt. calls it the greatest slaughter of Greeks he knew (3,000 Rhegines, Tarentines uncounted). 'Kailia' (Ceglie Messapica) is a modern label used by Wikipedia, not an ancient attestation.

name: Tegea
note: Second of the seer Tisamenus' five victories; date only roughly fixed between Plataea and Dipaea.

name: Akragas
note: Hieron marched on Akragas; Thrasydaeus' 20,000 mercenaries, Akragantines and Himeraeans lost over 4,000 (Syracusans c. 2,000). Exact site not given.

name: Dipaea
note: Sparta against all the Arcadians except the Mantineans. 'Arcadians' used as a new name since no Arcadian League existed yet (merge with Arcadian League if preferred).

name: Mycenae
note: Diodorus says the Argives defeated the Mycenaeans in battle before besieging and destroying the city; the siege itself is excluded. 'Mycenae' is a new entity name.

name: Eurymedon
place: banks of the river Eurymedon near Aspendus, Pamphylia
note: Land victory won the same day as the sea battle. Diodorus' version (a night attack with men in Persian dress) is generally rejected.

name: Eurymedon (sea)
place: off the mouth of the Eurymedon, Pamphylia
note: Diodorus places the naval battle off Cyprus. Plutarch adds a third action in which Cimon destroyed 80 Phoenician reinforcements at Hydrus (Cyprus); not counted separately.

name: Syracuse (sea)
note: Thrasybulus lost many triremes and fell back to Ortygia.

name: Syracuse
note: Thrasybulus led his army out of Achradina, was defeated, then negotiated his departure to Locri; end of the Deinomenid tyranny.

name: Thasos
note: Plutarch: 33 Thasian ships captured. The ensuing siege (465–463) is excluded.

name: Drabescus
note: The 10,000 colonists of Ennea Hodoi were destroyed by the Edonians and other Thracians. Herodotus places Sophanes' death at Datum, fighting the Edonians over the gold mines.

name: Ithome
place: Messenia (manuscripts: 'at the Isthmus'; usually emended to Ithome)
note: Fourth of Tisamenus' five victories, 'against the Messenians'; site and date uncertain. The long siege of Ithome is excluded.

name: Stenyclerus
note: Arimnestus (who killed Mardonius at Plataea) and 300 Spartans were killed fighting 'all the Messenians'. Known only from this passage; generally accepted as historical.

name: Syracuse (sea)
faction_b: Gelon's former mercenaries ('new citizens') holding Achradina and Ortygia
note: Site not specified beyond Syracuse.

name: Syracuse
note: Pitched battle won by the citizens; 600 picked men rewarded. Earlier street fighting (Diod. 11.73) not counted.

name: Oenoe
place: Oenoe, on the road from Argos to Mantinea, Argolid
note: Known only from Pausanias (painting in the Stoa Poikile; Argive group at Delphi). Thucydides is silent; some scholars think the monuments really commemorated Tanagra, or doubt the battle altogether.

name: Nile
war: Revolt of Inaros (Athenian expedition to Egypt)
note: Only Ctesias: an Athenian fleet (40 ships) defeated 50 Persian ships, taking 20 and sinking 30. Thucydides 1.104 only says the Athenians sailed up the Nile and took most of Memphis.

name: Papremis
war: Revolt of Inaros (Athenian expedition to Egypt)
sources: Hdt. 3.12.4, 7.7; Diod. 11.74; Ctesias FGrH 688 F14.36; Thuc. 1.104
note: Diodorus places the Persian defeat near Memphis and the White Fortress; Athenian presence is from Diodorus and Ctesias.

name: Hyria
note: Attested only by the Tarentine victory dedication at Delphi (Onatas and Calynthus) from spoils of the Peucetii, whom Opis had come to help. 'Hyria' (Oria) and the date c. 460 come from modern accounts (Wikipedia), not ancient sources.

name: Halieis
note: Thucydides: Corinthians and Epidaurians won; Diodorus claims an Athenian victory. 'Epidaurus' is a new entity name.

name: Cecryphaleia
note: Thucydides says only 'a Peloponnesian fleet'; Corinth assumed as leader.

name: Aegina
note: Athenians captured 70 ships, then besieged Aegina (siege excluded; it surrendered 457/6).

name: Megara
note: Fought by Athens' oldest and youngest reservists; close, both sides thought themselves not worsted, but Thucydides says the Athenians had the better and set up a trophy after the Corinthians withdrew.

name: Cimolia
date: 459/458 BCE (twelve days after the first battle)
note: The Corinthians returned to set up a rival trophy and were routed; a body of them trapped in an enclosure was stoned to death. Name 'Cimolia' from Diodorus.

name: Tanagra
note: Thessalian cavalry deserted the Athenians during the battle. Heavy losses on both sides; Diodorus calls it indecisive, but Thucydides and the Spartan dedication at Olympia give Sparta the victory.

name: Oenophyta
note: Athens then controlled Boeotia (except Thebes, per Diodorus), Phocis and Opuntian Locris.

name: Memphis
war: Revolt of Inaros (Athenian expedition to Egypt)
note: Megabyzus' relief army defeated the Egyptians and their allies, raised the siege of the White Fortress and drove the Greeks onto Prosopitis (the 18-month siege of Prosopitis is excluded).

name: Sicyon
note: Battle during Tolmides' raid around the Peloponnese (after the burning of Gytheum and capture of Chalcis).

name: Mazarus
place: land along the river Mazarus, western Sicily
note: Diodorus says Egesta fought 'the Lilybaeans' (Lilybaeum did not yet exist; usually emended to Selinuntines, though Motyans/Carthaginians are possible). Heavy losses on both sides, no victor named. Inclusion uncertain.

name: Mendesian mouth
war: Revolt of Inaros (Athenian expedition to Egypt)
place: Mendesian mouth of the Nile (Lake Manzala area)
note: A relief squadron of 50 Athenian and allied triremes, unaware Prosopitis had fallen, was attacked from land and by the Phoenician fleet; most ships were destroyed. The land arm took part.

name: Sicyon
place: by the river Nemea, territory of Sicyon
note: Plutarch places the rout of the Sicyonians 'by the Nemea'. Pericles then failed to take Sicyon or Oeniadae.

name: Oeniadae
note: Known only from Pausanias: the Messenians of Naupactus took Oeniadae, then fought the Acarnanians in the open; the fight was evenly balanced until night, after which they were besieged and broke out. Date and historicity doubtful.

name: Motyum
place: Motyum (prob. Vassallaggi, near San Cataldo), central Sicily
note: Relief battle during Ducetius' siege of the Akragantine fort; the Syracusan general Bolcon was later executed for alleged collusion.

name: Nomae
note: Ducetius' army routed; meanwhile Akragas retook Motyum. Ducetius later surrendered at Syracuse.

name: Salamis in Cyprus
note: After Cimon's death at Kition (siege excluded) the fleet won on land and at sea off Salamis against Phoenicians, Cypriots and Cilicians. Diodorus instead puts the land battle in Cilicia against Megabyzus.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (sea)
note: Persian side: Phoenician, Cypriot and Cilician ships. Diodorus: 100 ships captured.

name: Coronea
note: Victors were Boeotian oligarchic exiles (from Orchomenus etc.), counted under 'Thebes' as the Boeotians. Athens gave up Boeotia.

name: Himera River
place: river Himera (southern Himera, mod. Salso?), Sicily
note: War over Syracuse's release of Ducetius; over 1,000 Akragantines killed. Which Himera river (Salso or Grande) is uncertain.

name: Tragia
place: off the island of Tragia (prob. Agathonisi), south of Samos
note: 44 Athenian ships beat 70 Samian (20 of them transports) returning from Miletus.

name: Samos (sortie)
place: off Samos town and the Athenian naval camp
note: While Pericles was away towards Caria, the blockaded Samians sallied, destroyed the guard ships and beat the ships that put out against them, holding the sea for 14 days. Aristotle (in Plut.) says Pericles himself had earlier lost to Melissus.

name: Samos
note: After Athenian, Chian and Lesbian reinforcements arrived, 'the Samians fought a brief sea battle' but could not hold out and were besieged into surrender in the ninth month. Minor; inclusion is a judgement call. 'Mytilene' stands for the Lesbian contingent.

name: Leucimne
place: sea between Actium and Corcyra (trophy set up on Cape Leucimne, Corfu)
note: 80 Corcyraean ships destroyed 15 of 75 Corinthian ships. Thucydides says the Corinthians had reached Actium; the battle site is not stated (perhaps off Actium or further north), the trophy was on Leucimne. Epidamnus surrendered the same day (siege excluded).

name: Sybota
war: Corinthian–Corcyraean war (prelude to the Peloponnesian War)
place: off the Sybota islands and Cape Cheimerion, Thesprotia
commanders_b: Meikiades, Aisimides, Eurybatus (Corcyra); Lacedaemonius, Diotimus, Proteas (Athens)
note: Corinth (150 ships) routed the Corcyraeans (110) and the 10 Athenian ships, sinking c. 70, but withdrew when 20 more Athenian ships arrived; both sides set up trophies. Wikipedia calls it indecisive; scored here as a Corinthian battlefield victory.

name: Potidaea
war: Revolt of Potidaea (prelude to the Peloponnesian War)
place: isthmus north of Potidaea, Pallene, Chalcidice
note: Corinthian volunteers under Aristeus with the Potidaeans were defeated outside the town; the Macedonian rebels Philip and Pausanias fought with the Athenians, and the Chalcidians at Olynthus tried to help Potidaea. The siege that followed is excluded. 'Potidaea' is a new entity name.

name: Plataea
place: inside the city of Plataea, Boeotia
note: Theban night surprise attack, let in by Plataean oligarchs; the Plataeans rallied and defeated the c. 300 Thebans in street fighting, capturing 180 (later executed). Opening action of the war.

name: Lycia
note: Melesander, sent with 6 ships to collect money and protect shipping, marched inland into Lycia and was defeated and killed with part of his force. Minor.

name: Spartolus
commanders_b: Xenophon son of Euripides, Hestiodorus, Phanomachus (all killed)
note: Athenian hoplites beat the Chalcidian hoplites, but Chalcidian cavalry and light troops then routed the Athenians, killing 430 and all three generals. Site of Spartolus not precisely located.

name: Stratus
note: The Stratians ambushed and routed the advancing Chaonian and other Epirote 'barbarian' column before the city; Cnemus' army withdrew next day. Epirote tribes formed a large part of the defeated force.

name: Rhium
place: Gulf of Patras, off Patrae / Chalcis, near the mouth of the Corinthian Gulf
note: Phormio's first battle (also called Patrae or Chalcis): 20 Athenian triremes against 47 Peloponnesian ships formed in a defensive circle; 12 captured.

name: Naupactus
place: off the coast between Rhium and Naupactus, Corinthian Gulf
note: Phormio's second battle: 20 Athenian vs 77 Peloponnesian ships. The Peloponnesians first drove nine Athenian ships ashore, but the last Athenian ship rammed a pursuer and the Athenians routed the enemy and recovered their ships. Both sides set up trophies; usually counted an Athenian victory.

name: Mytilene (sortie)
note: The Mytileneans attacked the Athenian camp in full force and had slightly the better of it, but did not hold the field and withdrew into the city.

name: Sandius
place: the Sandian hill, Meander plain, inland from Myus (Caria/Ionia)
note: Money-collecting expedition of 12 ships; Lysicles and many of his men killed. Site of the Sandian hill unidentified.

name: Corcyra (stasis)
place: city of Corcyra (agora, harbours and Hyllaic harbour)
note: Street battles over several days: the oligarchs first defeated the demos, which then won the decisive fight; the oligarchs fired the houses round the agora. Followed by the arrival of Nicostratus and later massacres.

name: Corcyra (sea)
place: sea off Corcyra, south of the city
note: 53 Peloponnesian ships vs 60 Corcyraean and 12 Athenian; the disorganised Corcyraeans lost 13 ships; the Athenian squadron covered their retreat. The Peloponnesians did not exploit the victory.

name: Mylae
war: Peloponnesian War (first Athenian expedition to Sicily)
note: Two Messanian tribes garrisoning Mylae ambushed the Athenian landing and were routed; Mylae and then Messana submitted.

name: Tanagra
note: The Athenians defeated the Tanagraeans and some Thebans who came out against them; a raid in force rather than a campaign of conquest.

name: Aegitium
note: Aetolian tribes (Apodotians, Ophioneis, Eurytanes etc.; the formal Aetolian League is later) used javelin-men to destroy Demosthenes' hoplite army; 120 Athenian hoplites killed.

name: Olpae
place: Olpae, near Amphilochian Argos, Ambracian Gulf
note: Demosthenes' ambush in a sunken road rolled up Eurylochus' left; the Ambraciots on the right won locally but were cut off. The Athenian contingent was small (Demosthenes, archers), the Acarnanians/Amphilochians the main force.

name: Idomene
place: the twin hills of Idomene, Amphilochia
note: Dawn surprise of the Ambraciot relief army, a few days after Olpae; Thucydides calls it the greatest disaster to befall a single Greek city in so few days. Exact site disputed.

name: Caicinus
war: Peloponnesian War (first Athenian expedition to Sicily)
place: river Caicinus, territory of Epizephyrian Locri
note: Laches landed and defeated c. 300 Locrians. Minor; identification of the Caicinus (border river of Locri and Rhegium, Paus. 6.6.4) uncertain.

name: Strait of Messina
war: Peloponnesian War (first Athenian expedition to Sicily)
place: Strait of Messina between Rhegium and Messana
note: 16 Athenian and 8 Rhegian ships beat 30+ Syracusan and allied ships (one lost). A follow-up action off Peloris cost the Athenians two ships.

name: Naxos
place: before Naxos, east coast of Sicily
note: The Messanians attacked Naxos; the Naxians sallied out as Sicels came down from the hills and routed the Messanians, killing over 1,000.

name: Messana
war: Peloponnesian War (first Athenian expedition to Sicily)
note: Sortie battle: the Messanians and Locrians routed most of the Leontine army, but the Athenians landed, drove them back into the city and set up a trophy. Mixed result.

name: Pylos
note: Preceded by two days of Spartan land-and-sea assaults on Demosthenes' fort, which failed. The Athenian fleet of c. 50 ships then defeated the Peloponnesian fleet inside the harbour, cutting off the Spartiates on Sphacteria.

name: Sphacteria
place: island of Sphacteria (last stand at its northern hill), Pylos
note: Light troops wore down the 420 hoplites; 292 surrendered, about 120 of them Spartiates.

name: Solygeia
note: Hard-fought hoplite and cavalry battle; the Athenian cavalry decided it; 212 Corinthians and fewer than 50 Athenians killed.

name: Cythera
place: before the upper city of Cythera (with landing at Scandea)
note: The Cytherians (Lacedaemonian perioikoi with a Spartan governor) drew up against the landing, held briefly and fled to the upper town, which capitulated. Minor.

name: Megara
note: After the Athenians took the Long Walls and Nisaea, Brasidas' relief army arrived; a cavalry battle between the Boeotian and Athenian horse was indecisive (both claimed it; the Athenians set up a trophy). The Athenians then declined a pitched battle and Megara stayed with the Peloponnesians; Wikipedia calls it a Spartan (strategic) victory.

name: Delium
place: near Delium, on the Boeotian–Oropian border
note: Deep Theban phalanx and a cavalry flank attack broke the Athenians; c. 1,000 Athenian hoplites killed. The Boeotians then retook Delium by siege.

name: Sicyon
note: The Sicyonians attacked Demosthenes' landing before all his ships were ashore and drove the troops back to the ships, killing and capturing some; they set up a trophy. Minor.

name: Lyncestis
note: After a cavalry clash, the Lyncestian hoplites were routed and fled to the heights. Site within Lyncestis unknown; the plain is divided between Greece and North Macedonia.

name: Lyncestis (retreat)
place: pass leading from Lyncestis toward Arnisa
note: When the Illyrians changed sides, the Macedonians fled by night; Brasidas withdrew in hollow square, repelled every attack and stormed the hill commanding the pass, reaching Arnisa. Tactical success for Brasidas, but the invaders were forced out (Wikipedia: Lyncestian–Illyrian victory); scored here as a draw. Brasidas beat off every attack and reached Arnisa; the campaign failed because the Macedonians fled.

name: Mende
note: The Athenian attack on the 700 Mendaean, Scionaean and Peloponnesian hoplites on the hill was beaten off and the Athenians narrowly escaped defeat; days later stasis in Mende let the Athenians into the city.

name: Scione
note: The Athenians stormed the hill held by the Scionaeans and Peloponnesians, set up a trophy and began to wall off the city (siege until 421 excluded).

name: Laodocium
place: Laodocium (Ladoceia) in the Oresthis, near later Megalopolis, Arcadia
note: Each side's wing routed the opposing wing; both set up trophies and sent spoils to Delphi. Site unlocated.

name: Amphipolis
place: outside the walls of Amphipolis, Thrace
note: Brasidas' surprise sortie caught the Athenians withdrawing; c. 600 Athenians and 7 of Brasidas' men killed. Both commanders' deaths opened the way to the Peace of Nicias.

name: Cumae
note: The Campanians defeated the Cumaeans in battle, destroying most of their army, then took the city by storm (siege excluded). Diodorus dates it 421/0, Livy 420.

name: Heraclea Trachinia
note: The neighbouring peoples defeated the Spartan colony and killed its Lacedaemonian governor; Thebes took over Heraclea the next summer (Thuc. 5.52).

name: Mantinea
place: plain south of Mantinea, near the Pelagos wood, Arcadia
commanders_b: Laches and Nicostratus (Athenians, both killed); Argive generals
note: Largest hoplite battle of the war. The Mantineans and Argive picked Thousand broke the Spartan left, but the Spartan centre and right routed the rest and decided the day.

name: Argos (stasis)
note: The Argive demos rose against the oligarchy set up after Mantinea and won a battle in the city before Spartan help arrived; some oligarchs killed, others exiled.

name: Segesta
place: disputed border land between Selinus and Segesta, western Sicily
note: The Selinuntines won 'a fierce battle', killing many Egestaeans, who then appealed to Athens (prelude to the Sicilian Expedition). Site and exact year uncertain.

name: Syracuse (Anapus)
place: between the Anapus and the Olympieum, south of Syracuse
note: First battle at Syracuse (also 'Olympieum'): the Athenians, landed by a ruse, routed the Syracusans in a thunderstorm; Syracusan cavalry prevented a pursuit.

name: Epipolae
note: The Athenians seized Epipolae by surprise and routed the Syracusan counter-attack, killing Diomilus and c. 300 Syracusans.

name: Syracuse (first counter-wall)
place: Syracusan counter-wall below the Athenian 'Circle', near the Temenites
note: 300 picked Athenians and light troops stormed the stockade and routed its guard, though some pursuers were killed at the Temenites outwork; the counter-wall was destroyed. Small, field-works action.

name: Syracuse (Lysimeleia marsh)
place: marsh (Lysimeleia) below Epipolae, by the Great Harbour
note: The Athenians took the second counter-stockade across the marsh and routed the Syracusans, but Lamachus was killed in a counter-attack; a simultaneous Syracusan assault on the Circle was beaten off by Nicias.

name: Epipolae (first battle with Gylippus)
note: Fought in a cramped space where the Syracusan cavalry could not act; Gylippus took the blame. Sparta listed for Gylippus' command.

name: Epipolae (second battle with Gylippus)
place: open ground between the walls on Epipolae
note: Syracusan cavalry routed the Athenian left; the Syracusan counter-wall was then carried past the Athenian wall, ending the encirclement.

name: Syracuse (Great Harbour, Plemmyrium)
place: Great Harbour of Syracuse and mouth of the harbour
note: First naval battle in the harbour: the Athenians sank 11 Syracusan ships for 3 lost, but meanwhile Gylippus stormed the Athenian forts on Plemmyrium (land action), capturing the Athenian stores.

name: Mycalessus
place: between Mycalessus and the Euripus, Boeotia
note: After the Dii mercenaries (hired by Athens, led by an Athenian) massacred Mycalessus, Theban cavalry and hoplites caught them; the Thracians fought skilfully but lost c. 250 of 1,300, the Thebans c. 20. The massacre itself is not counted.

name: Erineus
place: off Erineus in Achaean Rhypice, Corinthian Gulf
note: Corinthian ships with reinforced bows disabled 7 Athenian ships for 3 of their own; both sides set up trophies (the Corinthians counted not being beaten a victory).

name: Syracuse (Great Harbour, second battle)
note: Two days of fighting; on the decisive day the Syracusans, with strengthened bows and a surprise meal-time attack (Ariston's plan), sank or disabled 7 Athenian ships.

name: Epipolae (night battle)
note: Demosthenes' night assault took the Syracusan fort and drove back Gylippus, but the Boeotians stood and routed the disordered Athenians; 2,000–2,500 Athenians and allies killed.

name: Euesperides
note: Peloponnesian hoplites bound for Syracuse were blown to Libya and relieved Euesperides, besieged by Libyans, defeating them. Composition of the force (helots/neodamodes and Boeotians from Taenarum?) inferred from Thuc. 7.19.

name: Syracuse (Great Harbour, third battle)
place: Great Harbour of Syracuse, inner bay by Lysimeleia
note: After the eclipse of 27 Aug. 413 delayed the Athenian departure; the Syracusans destroyed 18 Athenian ships and trapped the fleet. On shore the Etruscans and Athenians drove Gylippus' men into the marsh; both sides set up trophies.

name: Syracuse (Great Harbour, final battle)
place: Great Harbour of Syracuse, before the blocked harbour mouth
note: c. 110 Athenian vs c. 76 Syracusan ships fighting in a crowded harbour; the Athenian breakout failed and the crews refused to try again, forcing the land retreat.

name: Acraean Cliff
place: pass at the Acraean Cliff (Akraion Lepas) on the road to Acrae
note: During the retreat (after forcing the Anapus crossing) the Athenians tried for two days to storm the walled pass and were driven back by missiles and cavalry, then turned south toward the Helorine road. Inclusion as a separate battle is a judgement call; site identification uncertain.

name: Polyzelus' farm
place: walled olive grove on Polyzelus' estate, near the Erineus, south of Syracuse
note: Demosthenes' rearguard division was surrounded and shot at all day, then surrendered (6,000 men). Site name from Plutarch.

name: Assinarus
place: crossing of the Assinarus (Asinaro/Falconara) river, near Noto
note: Nicias' thirst-maddened division was slaughtered in the river bed and surrendered; end of the Sicilian Expedition. Some identify the Assinarus with the Tellaro instead.

name: Spiraeum
place: off Spiraeum (Peiraeus), deserted harbour on the Corinthian–Epidaurian border
note: The Athenians intercepted 21 Peloponnesian ships sailing for Chios, chased them into Spiraeum and fought on sea and land, disabling most of them; the survivors were blockaded.

name: Spiraeum (breakout)
note: The 20 blockaded Peloponnesian ships broke out, beat the equal Athenian blockading squadron and captured four ships.

name: Mytilene
note: The Athenians sailed into the harbour, beat the Chian ships, then landed, won a fight against the defenders and recovered the city. Harbour battle plus capture; minor.

name: Bolissus
note: Athenian landings at Cardamyle and Bolissus beat the Chians who came out, followed by two further victories at Phanae and Leuconium; grouped here as one entry. Raiding battles; minor.

name: Miletus
note: The Milesians routed the Argives (c. 300 killed), but the Athenians beat the Peloponnesians and Persians and held the field, then withdrew when a Peloponnesian–Syracusan fleet arrived.

name: Syme
note: Fought in rain and fog; Charminus attacked the Peloponnesian ships he could see, was surprised by the rest and lost 6 ships.

name: Chios (sortie)
place: Athenian fortified camp at Delphinium, Chios
note: Pedaritus' sortie took part of the Athenian wall and some beached ships, but the Athenian counter-attack routed the Chians and mercenaries; Pedaritus and many Chians killed.

name: Chios (sea)
note: 36 Chian and allied ships vs 32 Athenian; a stubborn fight in which the Chians 'had not the worse', then withdrew to the city at dusk.

name: Eretria
note: The hastily manned Athenian fleet was caught while its crews foraged (the Eretrians signalled the attack); 22 Athenian ships lost and Euboea revolted. Many fugitives were killed by the Eretrians.

name: Cynossema
place: Hellespont off Cynossema headland, between Sestos and Elaeus
note: 76 Athenian vs 86 Peloponnesian ships; after the Athenian centre was driven ashore, the Athenian wings routed the enemy. Taking 21 ships for 15 lost, it restored Athenian morale.

name: Abydos
note: Began with an Athenian attack on Dorieus' 14 ships near Rhoeteum/Dardanus; an all-day battle was decided by the arrival of Alcibiades with 18–20 ships; the Peloponnesians fled to the shore at Abydos, protected by Pharnabazus, losing c. 30 ships.

name: Cyzicus
place: off Cyzicus and on the shore near Cleri, Propontis
note: Combined sea and land battle: Alcibiades lured Mindarus out, the other squadrons cut him off, and the fight ended ashore against Pharnabazus' troops; the whole Peloponnesian fleet (c. 60 ships) taken or destroyed; two trophies.

name: Segesta
note: With 5,000 Libyans and 800 Campanians sent by Carthage, the Egestaeans fell on the Selinuntines scattered for plunder, killing c. 1,000; Diodorus dates it to 410/09 and treats it as the start of the Carthaginian war.

name: Corcyra (stasis)
note: After a democratic purge, oligarchic sympathisers seized the agora and recalled the exiles; fighting until nightfall ended in a negotiated reconciliation. Diodorus only; date per his archon year 410/09.

name: Pygela
note: Milesians coming to relieve Pygela routed scattered Athenian light troops, but Athenian peltasts and hoplites came up and killed almost all of them. Small engagement.

name: Ephesus
place: before Ephesus, near Coressus and the marsh
sources: Xen. Hell. 1.2.6–10; Diod. 13.64.1; Hell. Oxy. (Florence fragments)
note: Thrasyllus attacked in two divisions; the Ephesians, Tissaphernes' troops and the crews of 25 Syracusan and Selinuntine ships routed both, killing c. 300–400; two trophies set up.

name: Himera (sortie)
note: About 10,000 Himeraeans and allies (Diocles had brought 4,000 Syracusans and allies) sallied at dawn and routed the besiegers, but Hannibal's reserve counter-attacked and killed c. 3,000; Himera fell soon after. The siege itself is excluded.

name: Heraclea Trachinia
note: Betrayed by the (Phthiotic) Achaeans, the Heracleots lost c. 700 men and their Spartan harmost in battle with the Oetaeans. Some date 408.

name: Megara (Kerata)
place: the Kerata hills between Megara and Eleusis
note: After the Megarians recovered Nisaea, 1,000 Athenian foot and 400 horse defeated the Megarian levy and some Spartans, killing many Megarians and c. 20 Spartans. Diodorus only.

name: Abydos
note: Pharnabazus came with much cavalry to relieve Abydos; Alcibiades' cavalry and 120 hoplites routed him. A cavalry-dominated action.

name: Chalcedon
place: before the Athenian siege wall at Chalcedon, Bosporus
note: Sortie battle during the siege: Hippocrates' sortie was beaten by Thrasyllus' hoplites and Alcibiades' cavalry while Pharnabazus' relief force was kept off by the river and siege works. The siege itself is excluded.

name: Athens (walls)
place: outside the walls of Athens, by the Academy
note: Agis' night approach to Athens: the Athenian cavalry drove back the Boeotian and Peloponnesian horse at the walls; Agis then withdrew. Diodorus only; possibly related to Agis' approach of 410 (Xen. Hell. 1.1.33–34). Mainly a cavalry action.

name: Andros
note: The Andrians and their Lacedaemonian garrison came out against the Athenian landing and were routed into the city; the city itself was not taken.

name: Thasos (sortie)
note: Thrasybulus defeated the Thasians who came out against him, killing c. 200, then besieged the city until it accepted the exiles and an Athenian garrison. Battle detail from Diodorus only.

name: Eryx
note: About 40 Syracusan triremes met the 40-ship Carthaginian advance squadron and destroyed 15; the rest escaped at nightfall and the main Carthaginian fleet then secured the crossing.

name: Notium
place: off Notium, between Ephesus and Colophon
sources: Xen. Hell. 1.5.11–15; Diod. 13.71; Hell. Oxy. 4 (London fr.); Plut. Alc. 35, Lys. 5
note: Alcibiades' helmsman Antiochus provoked a fight against orders; Lysander took 15 (Xenophon) or 22 (Diodorus) ships. Led to Alcibiades' fall.

name: Cyme
note: The Cymaeans, reinforced from the countryside, attacked Alcibiades' raiding force, recovered the captives and drove the Athenians to their ships with loss. Diodorus/Nepos only; a repulse of a raid, included as borderline.

name: Akragas (relief battle)
place: near the Himeras river, on the approach to Akragas
note: The 30,000-strong relief army routed c. 40,000 of Himilco's troops, killing over 6,000, but did not pursue; the Akragantine generals failed to sally. Exact site disputed (Diodorus says as they crossed the Himeras). The siege itself is excluded.

name: Akragas (convoy battle)
place: south coast of Sicily near Akragas
note: 40 Carthaginian triremes from Panormus and Motya surprised the escort of the Syracusan grain convoy, sank 8 warships, drove the rest ashore and took the whole convoy, which doomed Akragas.

name: Mytilene
place: approaches to and harbour of Mytilene, Lesbos
note: Callicratidas (c. 170 ships) chased Conon's 70 into Mytilene, taking 30; Diodorus adds a second fight breaking the harbour barrier. Diomedon's relieving squadron of 12 was also caught (10 lost, Xen. 1.6.22). Led to the blockade relieved by Arginusae.

name: Arginusae
place: between the Arginusae islands and Cape Malea of Lesbos
allies_b: Peloponnesian and Ionian allies (incl. Boeotians, Euboeans)
commanders_a: Thrasyllus, Pericles the Younger, Diomedon, Erasinides, Aristocrates, Aristogenes, Lysias, Protomachus
note: Largest fleet battle between Greeks (c. 150 Athenian vs 120 Peloponnesian ships); the Peloponnesians lost c. 70 ships, the Athenians 25. Six victorious generals were executed for failing to rescue survivors.

name: Gela
note: Dionysius' three-pronged attack on the Carthaginian camp failed through poor coordination; the Italiote and Sicilian wings were beaten separately; Gela and Camarina were then evacuated. Earlier Geloan sorties are not counted separately.

name: Aegospotami
place: beach at Aegospotami, Thracian Chersonese, opposite Lampsacus
commanders_b: Conon, Philocles, Adeimantus, Menander, Tydeus, Cephisodotus
note: Lysander caught the Athenian fleet beached and its crews scattered; c. 170 of 180 ships taken (Conon escaped with 9); c. 3,000 prisoners executed. Decided the war.

name: Thessaly (Lycophron's victory)
note: Lycophron, aiming to rule all Thessaly, defeated the Larisaeans and other Thessalians opposing him, killing many; dated by Xenophon to about the time of the solar eclipse (3 Sept. 404).

name: Phyle
place: Spartan camp between Phyle and Acharnae, Attica
faction_b: the Thirty and their Spartan garrison
note: Dawn attack on the Spartan garrison and the Thirty's cavalry; about 120 hoplites killed. Dated 404/403; Diodorus puts it in 401/400.

name: Munychia
note: The Thirty had Spartan garrison troops with them.

name: Piraeus
note: Side B is the democrats of the Piraeus, not the city government (which sided with Sparta). Pausanias was checked at first (polemarchs Chaeron and Thibrachus killed) and then won; he then arranged the reconciliation that restored the democracy.

name: Porus
note: Side B is Clearchus, the renegade Spartan who made himself tyrant of Byzantium, with mercenaries. The site of Porus is unknown; Clearchus fled to Selymbria.

name: Syracuse (Neapolis)
place: outside Syracuse, near the Neapolis quarter
note: Dionysius, besieged on Ortygia, was relieved by 1,200 Campanian horse and then broke out and routed the rebels. Diodorus' year is 404/403, which straddles the batch boundary.

name: Elis
date: 402/401 BCE (Diodorus); the Elean war is c. 402–400
note: A sortie from the city. The Eleans and their 1,000 Aetolian helpers killed about 30 Lacedaemonians and the siege was raised. Xenophon reports no pitched battle in this war.

name: Cyrene
note: Heavy losses on both sides. The Messenians were almost all killed, and the factions then reconciled.

name: Motya (sea)
place: lagoon and outer sea off Motya
note: Himilco attacked the Greek ships in the lagoon. Dionysius hauled 80 triremes across the isthmus and repelled the attack with catapults from the shore, and Himilco withdrew. Some Greek ships were disabled. The siege of Motya itself is excluded.

name: Catana
note: Diodorus: over 100 Greek ships and 20,000 men lost.

name: Syracuse (Great Harbour)
note: While Dionysius was away, the Syracusan ships attacked the Carthaginian fleet escorting a grain convoy. They captured the flagship and destroyed 24 ships.

name: Syracuse
place: Carthaginian camp and forts at Polichna and Dascon, Syracuse
note: A combined land and sea attack on the plague-ridden Carthaginian camp, with the fleet burned at its moorings; Corinthian ships sank the last fugitives. A Spartan fleet under Pharacidas and Corinthian ships helped.

name: Sardis
place: plain near the Pactolus, outside Sardis
sources: Xen. Hell. 3.4.21–24; Hell. Oxy. 14 (Chambers); Diod. 14.80.1–5; Plut. Ages. 10
note: Xenophon describes a set battle against the Persian cavalry, while the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia and Diodorus describe an ambush.

name: Haliartus
place: below the walls of Haliartus, Boeotia
note: Lysander was killed. His troops then checked the Theban pursuit, which is why some modern works (e.g. Wikipedia) call the battle inconclusive. Athenian troops arrived only after the battle.

name: Naryx
note: About 1,000 Phocians and 500 Boeotians killed, per Diodorus.

name: Messana
note: The Messanians and Dionysius' mercenaries routed the Rhegine attack, killing over 500. Heloris was a Syracusan exile.

name: Nemea
place: by the Nemea river, between Sicyon and Corinth
note: Diodorus' losses: Spartan side 1,100, coalition about 2,800.

name: Agesilaus v Trallians
place: Thrace or Macedonia, on Agesilaus' route from the Hellespont
note: The Trallians demanded payment for passage. Agesilaus routed them. Their homeland (Thracian or Illyrian) and the site are uncertain, and the coordinates are a guess at the region.

name: Narthacium
place: between Mt Narthacium and Pras, south of Pharsalus, Thessaly
sources: Xen. Hell. 4.3.3–9; Xen. Ages. 2.2–5; Plut. Ages. 16.4
note: A cavalry battle won by Agesilaus' newly raised horse against the Thessalian (Pharsalian) cavalry.

name: Cnidus
note: The Athenian Conon commanded the Persian royal fleet as an exile in Persian service; Athens sent no ships. Isocrates credits Evagoras of Salamis with much of the force.

name: Coronea
place: plain below Coronea near the temple of Athena Itonia, Boeotia
sources: Xen. Hell. 4.3.15–21; Xen. Ages. 2.9–16; Plut. Ages. 18–19; Diod. 14.84.1–2
note: Agesilaus held the field and set up a trophy, but the Thebans broke through his line and Sparta did not follow up.

name: Abacaenum
note: Over 800 Carthaginians killed.

name: Corinth (Long Walls)
place: between the Long Walls of Corinth and Lechaeum
note: Corinthian oligarchic exiles let the Spartans inside the Long Walls. Diodorus has a second victory over the allied relief force (Boeotians, Athenians, Argives, Corinthians).

name: Lechaeum
sources: Xen. Hell. 4.5.11–17; Diod. 14.91.2; Plut. Ages. 22; Nep. Iphic. 2
note: Iphicrates' peltasts destroyed a Spartan mora, killing about 250 hoplites.

name: Sicyon
note: Only Diodorus reports it: about 500 Sicyonians killed. Minor.

name: Phlius
note: An ambush by Iphicrates' peltasts (Xenophon), counted as a battle by Diodorus (over 300 Phliasians killed). Borderline, included.

name: Maeander (Thibron)
note: Xenophon describes a cavalry surprise on Thibron's straggling force; Diodorus a battle in which most of the Spartan army fell.

name: Rhegium (sea)
note: Dionysius (50 ships) attacked 60 Crotoniate/Italiote ships, which fled to shore. Rhegine troops prevented him towing them off, and a storm then wrecked 7 of his ships. Indecisive.

name: Methymna
note: Diodorus misdates it to 392/391.

name: Acarnania
note: Agesilaus stormed the heights held by Acarnanian hoplites and peltasts, killed about 300 and set up a trophy. The Achaeans had asked for the campaign.

name: Cremaste
place: mountain road between Antandrus and Abydos near Cremaste, Troad
note: An ambush in which Anaxibius, 12 harmosts and about 200 men fell. Included as a battle by convention.

name: Laus
note: Over 10,000 Thurians and Italiote Greeks killed.

name: Lipari Islands
note: 10 Rhegine ships and their crews captured. A small action.

name: Elleporus
place: Elleporus river near Caulonia (Stilaro or Galliparo)
note: Over 10,000 Italiotes surrendered. Which modern river is the Elleporus is uncertain.

name: Zoster
place: landing place near Cape Zoster, Attica
note: A night attack on Eunomus' squadron as it landed; 4 Athenian triremes taken. A small action.

name: Aegina
note: Chabrias' ambush killed Gorgopas, 8 Spartiates and about 150 Aeginetans. An ambush, included as a battle; borderline.

name: Hellespont (Antalcidas)
note: Antalcidas ambushed and captured an Athenian squadron of 8 ships. A small action, but it gave Sparta control of the Hellespont.

name: Mantinea
note: The fight in which Pelopidas and Epaminondas were wounded fighting for Sparta. Part of the Spartan wing was routed and Agesipolis rescued them. The date and context are disputed, and the siege ended in Spartan success. Borderline.

name: Epirus (Molossians)
note: Dionysius I sent 2,000 men and armour to the Illyrians to restore the Molossian claimant Alcetas. Diodorus: over 15,000 Molossians killed. Sparta then intervened.

name: Pharos
note: Against Illyrian (Liburnian/Iadasinoi) light craft besieging the new Parian colony; over 5,000 killed and 2,000 captured. Fought partly at sea and partly ashore. 'Croatia' is a new country value. The Wikipedia list line wrongly gives a Liburnian victory; its article gives a Greek victory.

name: Pyrgi
note: A seaborne raid on the temple. The Caeretan relief force was defeated and many were taken prisoner.

name: Olynthus
note: Mainly a cavalry engagement. The Olynthians killed the hipparch Polycharmus but were driven into the city by Derdas' charge.

name: Olynthus
note: Diodorus: over 1,200 of Teleutias' army killed.

name: Citium
note: Evagoras (about 200 triremes) attacked first and had the upper hand until Glos' counterattack routed him. The siege of Salamis followed.

name: Cabala
note: Over 10,000 Carthaginians killed and 5,000 captured. The site is unidentified.

name: Thespiae
note: Phoebidas' sortie from Thespiae against retreating Theban raiders turned into a rout. Diodorus gives over 500 killed.

name: Thebes
note: Only Diodorus describes a battle, after which Agesilaus withdrew and the Thebans set up a trophy; Xenophon reports only skirmishing. Borderline.

name: Tanagra
note: Only Plutarch reports it. Minor.

name: Plataea
note: Only Plutarch reports it, in a list of minor Theban successes. Date approximate.

name: Cronium
note: Diodorus: over 14,000 Greeks killed. The site may be near Palermo or Monte Kronio at Sciacca.

name: Naxos
note: Diodorus: 24 Spartan ships destroyed and 8 captured, against 18 Athenian losses.

name: Abdera
note: The Triballi nearly annihilated the Abderites when Thracian allies changed sides. Earlier the Abderites had killed over 2,000 Triballian raiders on their way home. Chabrias then came and drove the invaders off. 'Abdera' is a new entity name.

name: Tegyra
place: pass near Tegyra, NE of Orchomenus, Boeotia
note: The Sacred Band, about 300 strong, broke a Spartan force about twice its size.

name: Alyzeia
place: off Alyzeia, Acarnanian coast opposite Leucas
note: Diodorus places it 'off Leucas'. Nicolochus withdrew and Timotheus set up a trophy, but the result was narrow.

name: Corcyra (sortie)
note: A sortie battle during the siege of Corcyra. Athenian peltasts under Ctesicles helped.

name: Corcyra (Syracusan squadron)
note: Iphicrates captured 9 of the 10 triremes Dionysius I sent to aid Sparta. A small action.

name: Orchomenus (Arcadia)
note: Xenophon says Mantineans; Diodorus says Arcadians. Polytropus' mercenaries were holding Orchomenus for Sparta.

name: Tegeatis–Laconia border
note: Only Diodorus reports it: the Argive column of Epaminondas' first invasion of Laconia forced the pass, killing Alexander and about 200 men. Minor.

name: Oeum
place: Oeum (Ion) in the Sciritis, north of Sparta
note: Ischolas' garrison held the pass to the last man against the Arcadian column.

name: Sparta
place: Eurotas crossing and outskirts of Sparta
note: Fighting at the Eurotas and the hippodrome, where a Spartan ambush routed the enemy cavalry. Epaminondas withdrew without taking the unwalled city. Diodorus calls it indecisive. Borderline.

name: Oneum
place: Spartan–Athenian lines on Mt Oneum, Isthmus of Corinth
note: Epaminondas broke through the Isthmus lines at the sector held by the Spartans and Pellenians. Plutarch calls it a victory over the Athenians near Cenchreae.

name: Corinth
note: The Thebans first drove the Corinthians inside the walls, then Chabrias repulsed their assault with heavy loss. Soon after, Dionysius I's Celtic and Iberian mercenaries skirmished with the Thebans nearby (Diod. 15.70.1; Xen. Hell. 7.1.20–22).

name: Tearless Battle
place: road junction to Eutresia and Melea, southern Arcadia
note: Named because no Spartan was said to have died. Dionysius I's auxiliaries under Cissidas served with Archidamus.

name: Eryx (harbour)
note: A surprise attack by about 200 Carthaginian ships captured most of Dionysius' 130 triremes in harbour.

name: Bosporus (Leucon v Heracleots)
note: The Heracleots landed from a large fleet and raided. Leucon posted Scythian archers behind his hoplites to cut down anyone who fled, then defeated the invaders. Date and site are uncertain.

name: Lasion
note: Over 200 Eleans killed. Diodorus has Athenian help for the Arcadians.

name: Cromnus
place: Arcadian siege lines at Cromnus, near Megalopolis
note: A relief battle during the Arcadian siege of the Spartan garrison in Cromnus. Archidamus was beaten off; a later night attack rescued part of the garrison.

name: Olympia
place: sanctuary of Olympia (the Altis), during the Olympic festival
note: Xenophon praises the Eleans, who drove the Arcadians and Argives back into the Altis but failed to take it and withdrew next day. Diodorus gives the victory to the Pisatans and Arcadians, who kept the sanctuary. Could be scored a draw.

name: Cynoscephalae
war: Theban campaigns against Alexander of Pherae
place: hills of Cynoscephalae near the Thetideion, Thessaly
note: Pelopidas brought only 300 horse; most of the force was the Thessalian League. Victory, but Pelopidas fell. Some lists call it a draw.

name: Mantinea (cavalry battle)
date: 362 BCE, days before the main battle
note: Newly arrived Athenian cavalry beat off the Theban and Thessalian horse attacking Mantinea. Xenophon's son Gryllus fell here.

name: Sparta
sources: Xen. Hell. 7.5.10–14; Diod. 15.82.6–83.5; Plut. Ages. 34; Polyb. 9.8
note: Epaminondas' surprise march on Sparta was repulsed in fighting inside the town.

name: Mantinea
note: The Thebans won the field but Epaminondas fell and no pursuit followed. Both sides set up trophies (Xenophon calls it indecisive); scored as a Theban battlefield victory.

name: Peparethos
note: Alexander attacked the Athenian squadron after part of it had been detached, taking 5 Attic and 1 Peparethian triremes and 600 men.

name: Upper Macedon
note: Over 4,000 Macedonians killed. The site is unknown and could be in Greece or North Macedonia.

name: Epirus (Arybbas v Bardylis)
note: Arybbas evacuated non-combatants to Aetolia and fell on the Illyrians as they withdrew laden with booty. Only Frontinus reports it, and the date is approximate.

name: Methone
note: Athens sent Mantias with 3,000 hoplites (probably largely mercenaries) to back Argaeus. Philip caught Argaeus' column on its retreat to Methone and released the Athenian prisoners.

name: Paeonia
note: Diodorus says only that Philip defeated the Paeonians in battle.

name: Erigon Valley
note: Also called Lyncus Plain. Diodorus says over 7,000 Illyrians fell. The site is debated; the Monastir/Bitola plain and the Lake Ohrid area have both been proposed.

name: Chios
note: Combined attack: Chares on land, Chabrias forcing the harbour, where he was killed. Mausolus backed the rebels.

name: Syracuse (cross-wall)
note: A sortie battle during the siege of Ortygia.

name: Grabaei
note: Plutarch: Parmenion 'had conquered the Illyrians in a great battle', with the news reaching Philip as Alexander was born. That Grabos was the opponent is a modern inference (IG II² 127). Site and country unknown.

name: Embata
place: Embata, Chios strait off Erythraean territory
commanders_b: Chares (Iphicrates and Timotheus declined to engage)
note: Diodorus places it in the Hellespont and implies a storm prevented a full engagement. Chares attacked alone and lost ships.

name: Phaedriades
note: Diodorus tells it twice (a doublet). The opponents were the Ozolian Locrians of Amphissa.

name: Syracuse (sea, Philistus)
note: About 60 ships a side. Philistus was captured and killed (or killed himself).

name: Leontini road
place: river crossing between Syracuse and Leontini
note: Dion, driven out of Syracuse, turned on the pursuing Syracusans and routed them, then released the prisoners.

name: Syracuse (sea, Nypsius)
note: Some of Nypsius' supply ships were sunk and 4 triremes captured, but the supplies got through.

name: Syracuse (Dion's return)
note: Nypsius' night sorties broke out of Ortygia and sacked the city. Dion marched back from Leontini and routed them; Diodorus says over 4,000 were killed.

name: Locris (cavalry)
note: Phocian cavalry beat the Locrian and Boeotian cavalry. Diodorus' doublet (16.25.2–3) also mentions a Phocian loss of 20 men and a later Phocian win against Locrians helped by Boeotians.

name: Argolas
place: hill of Argolas, Locris (perhaps near Mendenitsa)
note: About 6,000 Thessalians and allies were defeated. The site is not certainly identified.

name: Neapolis (Acragantine)
place: Neapolis in the territory of Acragas (site unknown)
note: Plutarch: Dion 'was forced into an engagement, and was worsted'. Only Plutarch reports it.

name: Neon
place: wooded rough ground near Neon (Tithorea), Phocis
note: Philomelus threw himself from a cliff. Diodorus does not name the site; Pausanias does. The Theban commander is uncertain.

name: Chaeronea
note: The Thebans defeated Onomarchus while he besieged Chaeronea, and he withdrew to Phocis.

name: Thessaly (Phayllus)
note: The 7,000 Phocians sent to help Lycophron of Pherae were driven out of Thessaly.

name: Thessaly (Onomarchus' first victory)
place: Thessaly (site unknown; a crescent-shaped mountain position)
note: Polyaenus describes stone-throwers hidden on the heights. Diodorus reports two Phocian victories; this is the first.

name: Thessaly (Onomarchus' second victory)
note: The second of the two Phocian victories in Diodorus; Philip withdrew to Macedon. No details survive.

name: Hermaeum (Coronea)
note: Onomarchus defeated the Boeotians and took Coronea. Linking this to Aristotle's battle 'at the Hermaeum' is a modern inference.

name: Crocus Field
place: Crocus Field, coastal plain near Pagasae / Halos, Thessaly
note: Over 6,000 Phocians and mercenaries killed. Chares' Athenian squadron was offshore but did not fight.

name: Cephisus
note: Over 500 Phocians killed and at least 400 captured.

name: Coronea
note: 50 Phocians killed and 130 captured.

name: Orneae
note: Over 200 Argives killed. Phocian troops and cavalry from the exiled tyrants of Pherae served with Sparta.

name: Megalopolitan War (indecisive battle)
note: Diodorus calls the battle stubborn and undecided. The Argives then went home and Sparta stormed Helissus. 'Arcadian League' here means Megalopolis and its Arcadian allies.

name: Telphusa
note: Diodorus adds two later Theban successes and one Spartan victory, without sites or details (not listed separately), before an armistice.

name: Abae
note: A night attack on Phayllus' camp. Borderline.

name: Naryx
note: Phayllus routed the Boeotians who came to help the besieged Narycaeans, then took and razed Naryx.

name: Chaeronea
note: A cavalry battle. Just before it, a Boeotian night attack (site not given) killed Mnaseas and about 200 Phocians.

name: Tamynae
note: Callias' Chalcidians, with mercenaries sent by Philip, attacked Phocion's camp after Plutarch, tyrant of Eretria, turned against the Athenians.

name: Olynthus
note: Diodorus: Philip beat the Olynthians in two field battles (κατὰ δύο μάχας) and shut them in the city, which then fell by treachery. Counted as one entry.

name: Hyampolis
note: About 70 Phocians killed.

name: Coronea
note: Heavy Boeotian losses. Diodorus adds that the Boeotians lost more men in an attack on their return march after a later raid.

name: Abae
place: near the sanctuary of Apollo at Abae, Phocis
note: The Boeotians attacked Phocians fortifying a post near Abae. About 500 fugitives died when the temple they sheltered in caught fire.

name: Syracuse (Hicetas v Dionysius II)
note: Hicetas, a Syracusan ruling Leontini, turned on Dionysius' pursuit as he withdrew and killed over 3,000 mercenaries. He then took the city except Ortygia. In effect a Syracusan civil war; scored as Leontini v Syracuse (Dionysius' regime).

name: Illyria (Pleuratus)
note: Didymus: Philip was wounded in the leg pursuing Pleuratus, 150 Companions were wounded and Hippostratus was killed. Wikipedia makes it a defeat for Philip. The result is unclear and scored indecisive.

name: Hadranum
note: Timoleon's roughly 1,200-man Corinthian expedition, mostly mercenaries, surprised Hicetas' 5,000 at dinner: about 300 killed, 600 captured and the camp taken.

name: Syracuse (Neon's sortie)
note: While Mago and Hicetas were away attacking Catana, the Corinthian garrison of Ortygia sortied, routed the besiegers left behind and took Achradina.

name: Syracuse (Timoleon's assault)
place: Hicetas' positions at Syracuse (Epipolae, Achradina, river bank)
note: After Mago's fleet left, Timoleon stormed Hicetas' positions from three sides, reportedly without losing a man, and took Syracuse. This is the battle within Wikipedia's 'Siege of Syracuse (343 BC)'.

name: Illyria (Caeria)
note: Philip's daughter Cynane killed the Illyrian queen in battle. Only Polyaenus tells it, and the date is a modern estimate. Site and country unknown.

name: Lyctus
note: Phalaecus' former Phocian mercenaries, hired by Cnossus, had taken Lyctus. Archidamus beat them on his way to Italy and restored the Lyctians. Side B = Cnossus' mercenaries; allies A = the Lyctian exiles.

name: Elis
faction_b: Elean exiles with Phalaecus' former Phocian mercenaries
note: Many mercenaries killed and about 4,000 captured. The Eleans executed their prisoners as temple-robbers.

name: Crimisus
place: river Crimisus, western Sicily (Freddo or Belice)
note: The Carthaginian Sacred Band was destroyed. Timoleon was a Corinthian general commanding Syracusans and mercenaries. Which modern river the Crimisus is is disputed.

name: Messana (territory)
note: 400 of Timoleon's mercenaries were killed by Gisco's force, which was allied with Mamercus of Catana and Hicetas. Minor.

name: Ietae
note: An ambush that cut Euthymus' raiding mercenaries to pieces. Borderline.

name: Ateas (Scythians)
place: Dobruja, south of the Danube delta
sources: Justin 9.2; Frontin. Str. 2.8.14; Strabo 7.3.18; Lucian Macr. 10
note: About 20,000 women and children reportedly captured. Site unknown.

name: Triballi
note: The Triballi attacked Philip's army on its way home from Scythia, wounded him in the thigh and took the Scythian booty. Some scholars treat it as an indecisive running fight.

name: Damurias
place: crossing of the river Damurias, eastern Sicily
note: About 1,000 of Hicetas' men were killed as he returned from raiding Syracusan territory. The river is unidentified.

name: River Battle
war: Fourth Sacred War (Philip v Athens and Thebes)
place: by a river in Phocis (Cephisus valley?), site unknown
note: Demosthenes names 'the battle by the river' as an Athenian–Theban success. Probably a minor engagement; there are no details.

name: Winter Battle
war: Fourth Sacred War (Philip v Athens and Thebes)
note: Demosthenes' 'winter battle', an Athenian–Theban success. Probably minor; there are no details.

name: Amphissa
war: Fourth Sacred War (Philip v Athens and Thebes)
place: pass from Cytinium to Amphissa (Gravia pass)
note: Philip let a false letter be captured, then surprised and destroyed the 10,000 mercenaries holding the pass for Athens and Thebes, and took Amphissa.

name: Chaeronea
war: Fourth Sacred War (Philip v Athens and Thebes)
sources: Diod. 16.85.2–86.6; Plut. Alex. 9; Plut. Dem. 19–20; Polyaenus 4.2.2, 4.2.7; Justin 9.3.4–11

name: Manduria
date: August 338 BCE (said to be the same day as Chaeronea)
sources: Diod. 16.63.1–2, 16.88.3–4; Plut. Agis 3.2; Paus. 3.10.5; Theopompus FGrH 115 F232
note: Archidamus led a Spartan force, largely mercenaries, in Tarentine service. Diodorus names only the Lucanians; Plutarch and Pausanias name the Messapians at Manduria. Sparta is counted as principal because a Spartan king commanded.

name: Abolus
place: stream of the Abolus near Catana
note: Over 2,000 of Mamercus' men killed, many of them Gisco's Carthaginian auxiliaries. The river is unidentified.

name: Illyria (Pleurias)
note: Diodorus says only that a Pausanias died shielding Philip. The result is not recorded (Wikipedia: Illyrian victory) and is scored as unknown/indecisive. It may be the same campaign as the Pleuratus entry. Site and country unknown.

name: Magnesia
place: near Magnesia (probably on the Maeander), Ionia
note: Memnon (c. 4,000) feigned withdrawals, then fell on the Macedonian advance force (10,000) when it had stood down; many killed or captured, the rest fled into Magnesia. Usually taken as Magnesia on the Maeander, some prefer Magnesia ad Sipylum. Dated before Attalus' murder (late 336/early 335).

name: Troad
note: Calas with Macedonians and mercenaries fought a much larger Persian force, was worsted and fell back on Rhoeteum; site unknown.

name: Mount Haemus
note: 'Autonomous Thracians' held the ridge behind a wagon laager and rolled the carts down on the phalanx; c. 1,500 killed. Pass identification uncertain (often the Shipka pass).

name: Lyginus
place: wooded glen by the river Lyginus, land of the Triballi
note: Against the Triballi (king Syrmus had withdrawn to Peuce island); c. 3,000 Triballi killed. The Lyginus is identified (CAH) with the Rositsa, a tributary of the Yantra; exact site unknown.

name: Danube
place: north bank of the lower Danube, land of the Getae
note: Against the Getae (reportedly 4,000 cavalry, 10,000 infantry), who fled after the first cavalry charge following Alexander's night crossing on hide floats; their town was taken. Crossing site unknown. The failed assault on Peuce island is excluded.

name: Pelium
place: Pelium (Pelion), west of Small Prespa lake, Dassaretis
commanders_b: Cleitus son of Bardylis, Glaucias of the Taulantii
note: Includes the drill-parade breakout across the Eordaicus and the night attack three days later that routed Cleitus and Glaucias. Alexander's siege of Pelium itself was abandoned. Site: Hammond near Goricë; others elsewhere west of the Prespa lakes.

name: Thebes (before the walls)
note: Diodorus describes a long pitched battle before the city, broken when Perdiccas entered by an unguarded postern. Arrian has an assault on the outer palisade instead. The city was then stormed and razed (the sack itself is not counted). Allies of Alexander: Phocians, Plataeans, Thespians, Orchomenians.

name: Granicus
commanders_b: Arsites, Spithridates, Rhoesaces, Arsames, Memnon of Rhodes

name: Halicarnassus (sortie)
place: before the walls of Halicarnassus, Caria
note: The garrison made several sorties. The largest, led by the Athenian exile Ephialtes from the Tripylon gate, became a full-scale battle that Macedonian veterans turned; Ephialtes fell. The siege itself is excluded.

name: Sagalassus
note: The Sagalassians and their Termessian allies held the hill in front of the city; c. 500 killed, Macedonian losses c. 20 including the officer Cleander. New entity name: Pisidians.

name: Siphnos
note: A small dawn surprise attack. Proteas with 15 ships captured 8 of Datames' 10 ships with their crews.

name: Caria
note: Arrian calls it a 'great battle': 700 infantry and 50 cavalry killed and at least 1,000 captured. Orontobates still held the Halicarnassus citadel, Myndus, Caunus and Cos. The news reached Alexander at Soli.

name: Issus
note: The Pinarus is usually identified with the Payas (Hammond, Devine); older view the Deli Çay.

name: Hellespont
note: Known from Curtius only. The Macedonian fleet summoned from Greece beat Aristomenes, sent by Darius to recover the Hellespontine coast, capturing or sinking his ships. Exact site and date unknown.

name: Lydia
place: Lydia / western Asia Minor (three separate sites)
note: One entry for three battles. Curtius says Persian commanders who escaped from Issus, with Cappadocian and Paphlagonian levies, tried to recover Lydia. Antigonus beat them in three battles 'in one region after another'. No sites are named.

name: Tyre (harbour battle)
note: A Tyrian squadron (13 ships) sallied at midday and sank the quinqueremes of the Cypriot kings Pnytagoras, Androcles and Pasicrates. Alexander's squadron then came round and cut it off. An earlier clash at the harbour mouth (3 Tyrian ships sunk) is folded in here. The siege itself is excluded. New entity name: Tyre (Phoenician).

name: Miletus
note: Uncertain inclusion. Curtius alone says Balacrus 'defeated Hydarnes, Darius' commander, and took Miletus again'. This may have been an assault rather than a field battle.

name: Gaza (sortie)
note: The garrison (with Arab mercenaries) sallied and burned the siege works. It was driven back, but Alexander was wounded by a catapult bolt. The siege itself is excluded.

name: Paestum
note: Livy says Alexander landed near Paestum and beat the Samnites and Lucanians in a pitched battle. Livy's Varronian year is followed here; he had been called in by Taras c. 334/333.

name: Peloponnese
note: Defeat of Corrhagus, Antipater's general in the Peloponnese. Aeschines says the Spartans and their mercenaries destroyed his force. No details or site survive.

name: Gaugamela
place: Gaugamela, plain east of the Tigris near Arbela
note: Exact site uncertain: Tell Gomel, or the Karamlesh plain east of Mosul.

name: Megalopolis
note: Agis was killed. Diodorus gives 5,300 dead on the Spartan side and 3,500 on Antipater's. Sparta's allies were Elis, the Achaeans (except Pellene) and the Arcadians (except Megalopolis). The date is disputed.

name: Pandosia
place: near Pandosia, by the river Acheron, Bruttium
note: Alexander's army, split across three hills by floods, was overwhelmed, and he was killed by a Lucanian exile while crossing the Acheron. Livy places it under 326, but the synchronism with Alexander the Great gives 331/330. The site of Pandosia Bruttia is uncertain (near Cosenza).

name: Scythia
place: Scythia, north-west of the Black Sea (site unknown)
note: Zopyrion, Alexander's governor in Thrace ('Pontus' in Justin), invaded Scythia with 30,000 men and besieged Olbia (Macrobius). He then perished with his whole army. Justin dates it c. 331; Curtius puts the news in 325. No details of the battle survive.

name: Uxian Defile
place: pass on the Susa–Persepolis road (Behbahan route), Zagros
note: Arrian: the mountain Uxians, who demanded toll, were turned out of the pass and routed into Craterus' blocking force. Curtius instead describes a siege of Madates' town. Exact site unknown. New entity name: Uxians.

name: Persian Gate
place: Persian Gates pass, Zagros, on the road to Persepolis
note: A first frontal assault was repulsed. Alexander then outflanked the walled pass by a mountain path. The site is usually placed near Cheshmeh Chenar (Tang-e Meyran); some prefer Tang-e Mohammad Reza.

name: Aria
note: Satibarzanes, the rebel satrap of Aria acting for Bessus (Artaxerxes V), was killed by Erigyius in single combat, and his army broke. 'Persia' here stands for Bessus' Achaemenid claimant regime.

name: Jaxartes
place: river Jaxartes (Syr Darya) near Alexandria Eschate (Khujand)
note: The sources call them Scythians; 'Saka' is used for the Central Asian Scythians in this batch.

name: Polytimetus
note: Spitamenes and his Scythian (Massagetan/Dahan) horse archers destroyed the relief column sent to Maracanda, killing c. 2,000 at the river crossing. Arrian gives two versions (Ptolemy and Aristobulus). New entity name: Sogdians.

name: Xenippa
place: Xenippa, on the Scythian border of Bactria-Sogdiana (unlocated)
note: Known from Curtius only. About 2,500 rebel Bactrian exile horsemen attacked Amyntas and lost 700 killed and 300 captured; Macedonian losses were 80 killed and 350 wounded. Site unknown. New entity name: Bactrians.

name: Gabai
place: near Gabai, Sogdian stronghold on the Massagetan border
note: Spitamenes attacked with 3,000 Massagetan horse and lost more than 800; the Massagetae then killed him. Curtius 8.3 tells a different story of his death. Gabai is unlocated.

name: Zariaspa
place: edge of the desert beyond Zariaspa (Bactra), Bactria (site unknown)
note: After Spitamenes' Massagetae ambushed the sortie of the Zariaspa garrison (Aristonicus killed, Peithon captured; that ambush is not listed), Craterus caught them near the desert, joined by more than 1,000 further Massagetan horse. Arrian calls it a hard-fought battle; about 150 Scythians fell and the rest escaped into the desert. Minor, but comparable to Xenippa and Gabai, which are listed.

name: Paraetacene
note: A hard-fought battle with the last rebel chiefs of Paraetacene. Catanes was killed and Austanes captured; 120 cavalry and 1,500 infantry of the rebels fell. 'Sogdians' stands for the Sogdian/Paraetacenian rebels.

name: Arigaeum
place: hills near Arigaeum, land of the Aspasians (Bajaur/Kunar)
note: Against the Aspasians. This entry combines the hill fight in which Ptolemy killed the Aspasian chief and the larger three-division battle near Arigaeum, after which 40,000 men and 230,000 oxen were captured (Ptolemy's figures via Arrian).

name: Massaga (sortie)
place: before Massaga, land of the Assacenians (lower Swat/Dir)
note: Against the Assacenians and their 7,000 Indian mercenaries. A feigned Macedonian retreat drew them out, and they were routed back into the city. The siege that followed is excluded. Site of Massaga uncertain.

name: Bazira (sortie)
note: Uncertain inclusion (small). The Bazirians came down into the plain against Coenus' garrison force; Arrian calls it a 'sharp battle', with c. 500 Indians killed and 70 captured. The town was afterwards abandoned for Aornos.

name: Hydaspes
place: left bank of the Hydaspes (Jhelum), Punjab
note: Indians = Porus' kingdom, with Taxiles' contingent on Alexander's side. Includes the defeat of Porus' son at the crossing. Crossing and battle site disputed: near Jhelum town, or the Jalalpur/Haranpur area.

name: Sangala (field battle)
place: hill before Sangala, land of the Cathaei (between Hydraotes and Hyphasis)
note: The Cathaei fought from a triple wagon laager on a hill before the city and were driven inside. The siege that followed is excluded. Sangala is unlocated (Sangla Hill is one guess).

name: Agalassi
place: land of the Agalassoi, near the Hydaspes–Acesines confluence
note: Diodorus says the Agalassoi (40,000 infantry, 3,000 cavalry) drew up in battle order and were beaten with heavy loss, after which their towns were stormed. Arrian does not mention it. Site unknown.

name: Hydraotes
place: east bank of the Hydraotes (Ravi), land of the Malli
