note: Against the Malli: about 50,000 drawn up beyond the river were pinned by Alexander's cavalry until the infantry came up, then fled into their strongest city. The siege in which Alexander was nearly killed is excluded.

name: Harmatelia (sortie)
place: before Harmatelia, a Brahmin city on the lower Indus
note: Uncertain inclusion. A feigned retreat by 500 light troops drew c. 3,000 defenders out, and they were cut up by Alexander. Ptolemy was wounded by a poisoned weapon, and the city later surrendered. Site unknown.

name: Oreitis
place: land of the Oreitae (Las Bela), Gedrosia
note: Against the Oreitae (an 'Indian' people for Arrian) and their neighbours, who attacked Leonnatus' rearguard division. Arrian's Indica gives 6,000 killed, including all their leaders. Site unknown.

name: Cyrene
note: Thibron, Harpalus' murderer, landed with c. 7,000 mercenaries guided by Cyrenaean exiles. He beat the Cyrenaeans, took the harbour and forced the city to pay 500 talents. New entity name: Thibron (mercenary army).

name: Cyrene
note: After the Cretan Mnasicles changed sides and Thibron lost his fleet, the Cyrenaeans engaged him and won, killing many. This came after he brought 2,500 mercenaries from Taenarum. Site not stated.

name: Plataea
note: Leosthenes with Athenians and mercenaries beat the pro-Macedonian Boeotians, who held former Theban land, before returning to Thermopylae. Some modern accounts add Euboeans and the Cadmea garrison. New entity name: 'Boeotians', not 'Thebes', because Thebes had been destroyed in 335.

name: Thermopylae
note: The Thessalian cavalry deserted Antipater for the Greeks. He was beaten and shut himself up in Lamia, and the siege of Lamia is excluded. The site is not given; the battle is conventionally named Thermopylae (Leosthenes' base).

name: Bactria
war: Revolt of the Greek settlers in the Upper Satrapies
note: Peithon led Macedonians sent by the regent Perdiccas against more than 20,000 infantry and 3,000 cavalry of the rebel colonists. The rebel Letodorus withdrew his 3,000 in mid-battle and the rest fled. The surrendered Greeks were then massacred. 'Perdiccas' (royal army) is used here before 321. New entity name: Greek settlers (Upper Satrapies).

name: Thrace
note: Lysimachus (4,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry) fought Seuthes (20,000 infantry, 8,000 cavalry) and lost many men but killed many more. Diodorus says he left with a doubtful claim to victory and both sides withdrew. Lysimachus was then Macedonian satrap of Thrace.

name: Melitaea
place: plain of southern Thessaly (perhaps near Melitaea)
note: Defeat and death of Leonnatus in a cavalry battle won by Menon's Thessalians; the Macedonian phalanx withdrew to high ground. The site is unknown: Yardley suggests Melitaea, Hammond only 'the open plain of Thessaly'. Diodorus says the Aetolians had already gone home.

name: Abydos
sources: IG II² 398a + 438; IG II² 493; cf. Diod. 18.15.8–9
note: Known from Athenian decrees about a naval battle in the Hellespont and help given to Athenian survivors. It is probably one of Diodorus' 'two naval battles'. The commanders are not named in the inscriptions; some doubt Cleitus commanded here.

name: Rhamnous
note: Phocion defeated a Macedonian and mercenary landing force that was ravaging the coast, killing Micion. It was a small action.

name: Echinades
place: near the Echinades islands, off Acarnania (identification disputed)
note: Diodorus says Cleitus beat Euetion in two battles and destroyed many ships near the Echinades. Bosworth makes it a separate Ionian Sea battle off Oiniadai in spring 322. Others emend to the Lichades (Malian Gulf) or treat it as a doublet of Amorgos/Abydos; it might be counted twice.

name: Amorgos
sources: Marm. Par. FGrH 239 B9; Plut. Demetr. 11.4; Plut. Mor. 338a; Diod. 18.15.8–9
note: The decisive defeat of the Athenian navy (c. 170 ships against 240), although Plutarch says only 3–4 Athenian ships were sunk.

name: Cappadocia
sources: Diod. 18.16.1–3; Arr. Succ. fr. 1.11; App. Mithr. 8; Plut. Eum. 3.12–14; Just. 13.6.1–3
note: Ariarathes (reportedly 30,000 infantry, 15,000 cavalry) was beaten: 4,000 killed and 5,000 captured, including the king, who was impaled. Diodorus describes one battle; some accounts mention more than one engagement. 'Perdiccas' (royal army) is used here before 321.

name: Crannon
sources: Diod. 18.17.1–5; Plut. Phoc. 26.1; Plut. Dem. 28.1; Plut. Cam. 19.8; Arr. Succ. fr. 1.12
note: The Greek cavalry had the upper hand, but the phalanx drove the Greek infantry from the field; about 500 Greek and 130 Macedonian dead. A limited tactical victory that decided the war. Aetolians absent.

name: Cyrene
note: The Cyrenaeans, reinforced by neighbouring Libyans and Carthaginians, fielded c. 30,000 men and were heavily defeated. Thibron renewed the siege, and the Cyrenaeans then made Mnasicles general.

name: Cyrene
note: Ptolemy sent Ophellas at the request of Cyrenaean exiles, and the Cyrenaean democrats joined Thibron. Diodorus says Ophellas 'defeated and captured' Thibron and took over the cities. In Arrian, Thibron was caught in flight by Libyans and executed at Taucheira (Apollonia in some accounts). There are no details of the battle.

name: Eumenes v Neoptolemus
place: Asia Minor, probably near Cappadocia (site unknown)
note: Eumenes commanded for the Perdiccan regency; Neoptolemus had come to terms with Antipater and fled to him with c. 300 horse. Site unknown; c. 10 days before the battle with Craterus.

name: Hellespont
place: Asia Minor; Diodorus says 'near Cappadocia' (site unknown)
sources: Diod. 18.30–32, 18.37.1; Plut. Eum. 6–7; Nep. Eum. 4; Arr. Succ. F 1.27
note: Conventional name from Eumenes' mission to guard the Hellespont; Diod. 18.37.1 places it near Cappadocia, Wikipedia near the Dardanelles. Craterus and Neoptolemus (killed by Eumenes in single combat) commanded for Antipater's coalition.

name: Camel's Fort
place: Fort of Camels on the Nile, eastern Delta
note: A day-long assault on a fortified post rather than a pitched battle; included as the main engagement of Perdiccas' invasion of Egypt. The later disaster at the Nile crossing near Memphis was not a battle; Perdiccas was then murdered by his officers.

name: Amphissa
war: First War of the Diadochi (Aetolian war)
note: Aetolians (allied to Perdiccas) besieging Amphissa defeated and killed Antipater's general Polycles; site not stated precisely.

name: Thessaly
war: First War of the Diadochi (Aetolian war)
note: Polyperchon, holding Macedon for Antipater, crushed the Thessalian rebels (allies of the Aetolians, who had gone home).

name: Rhodes
note: Attalus led the Perdiccan fleet after Perdiccas' death ('Perdiccas' here = the Perdiccan remnant); he had raided Cnidus and Caunus.

name: Caria
note: Asander, satrap of Caria, sent by the regent Antipater against the Perdiccan remnant and defeated. Only a one-line notice; site unknown.

name: Orcynia
note: Eumenes lost through the defection of his cavalry officer Apollonides; he was then besieged at Nora. Eumenes at this time was condemned as an outlaw, not yet the royal general.

name: Cretopolis
note: 'Perdiccas' here = the Perdiccan remnant under Alcetas. Attalus, Docimus and Polemon captured; Alcetas fled to Termessus.

name: Parthia (Peithon v the upper satraps)
note: Peucestas and the satraps of the upper provinces defeated Peithon, satrap of Media, after he had killed Philip of Parthia. Both sides Macedonian.

name: Byzantium (first battle)
note: Cleitus commanded the fleet of the regent Polyperchon (= Macedon); Nicanor led Cassander's fleet reinforced by Antigonus' ships and lost c. 70 ships. Wikipedia treats both engagements as one 'Battle of Byzantium (317 BC)'.

name: Byzantium (second battle)
place: European shore of the Bosporus near Byzantium
note: Combined dawn attack by land (light troops ferried over by the Byzantines) and sea two days after the first battle; Cleitus' fleet destroyed, Cleitus later killed by Lysimachus' men.

name: Coprates
place: crossing of the Coprates (Dez) river, Susiana
note: Eumenes surprised the part of Antigonus' army that had crossed the river; c. 4,000 captured. Coprates usually identified with the Dez.

name: Paraitacene
note: Eumenes' phalanx routed Antigonus' and Antigonus lost far more men, but Antigonus' cavalry broke Eumenes' left and Antigonus camped on the field and claimed victory. Wikipedia infobox: Eumenes victory; often judged indecisive.

name: Bisaltia
war: Second War of the Diadochi (Macedonian civil war)
note: Aristonous killed most of Crateuas' force and besieged him at Bedyndia in Bisaltia, where he surrendered. Fought while Cassander besieged Olympias in Pydna.

name: Gabiene
sources: Diod. 19.39–43; Plut. Eum. 16–17; Nep. Eum. 10; Polyaen. 4.6.13
note: Tactically mixed: Eumenes' Silver Shields routed Antigonus' phalanx, but Antigonus' cavalry won and captured the baggage; the Silver Shields then handed Eumenes over. Wikipedia: inconclusive, Antigonid overall victory.

name: Aphrodisias (Cilicia)
note: Combined ambush: Perilaus' land force caught first, then Theodotus' squadron (Rhodian-built ships) routed and all its ships captured.

name: Sicyon
note: Cratesipolis, widow of Alexander son of Polyperchon, crushed a rising of the Sicyonians 'with great slaughter' and crucified 30.

name: Hebrus (Illyria)
note: The river name is otherwise unknown (Loeb note); followed by a treaty with Glaucias.

name: Lemnos
note: Athens (under Demetrius of Phalerum) acted for its ally Cassander; Seleucus' Ptolemaic squadron had supported Aristotle but had left. Most Athenian ships captured.

name: Caprima
note: Midnight attack on the fortified camp of Cassander's general (c. 8,000 foot, 200 horse); included as the destruction of an army, though a surprise attack rather than a set battle.

name: Medius' sea victory
place: at sea on Medius' voyage from Phoenicia to Caria (site unknown)
note: Medius defeated and captured 36 ships of 'the Pydnaeans' (Cassander's partisans); the Loeb editor thinks the name corrupt. Site and opponent uncertain.

name: Callatis
war: Third War of the Diadochi (Lysimachus v Pontic cities)
note: Pitched battle against the Scythians who came to help rebel Callatis; the Thracians changed sides before the fighting. Followed by a siege of Callatis.

name: Haemus Pass
place: a pass of the Haemus (Balkan) mountains
note: Seuthes, allied with Antigonus, held the pass; long, hard-fought battle with heavy losses on both sides.

name: Hieron (Thrace)
note: Antigonus' relief force for Callatis caught in a place difficult of access; Pausanias killed, men ransomed or enrolled. Location of 'Hieron' unknown (Loeb); coordinates only indicate Thrace.

name: Epirus (Philip v Aeacides)
note: Philip intercepted Aeacides before he could join the Aetolians, killing many and capturing c. 50 leaders of the king's restoration.

name: Oeniadae
note: Site from Pausanias; Diodorus does not name it.

name: Oreus (first)
note: Antigonid relief fleet attacked Cassander's ships blockading Oreus and burned four. Small engagement; Wikipedia (Medius) dates it 312.

name: Oreus (second)
note: Reinforced by Athenian ships, Cassander counter-attacked, sank one Antigonid ship and captured three with crews. Small engagement.

name: Gaza
note: Seleucus fought as Ptolemy's officer; the victory let him return to Babylon.

name: Petra
war: Third War of the Diadochi (Antigonid–Nabataean war)
place: Athenaeus' camp c. 200 stades from Petra on his return march
note: After Athenaeus raided Petra while the men were away, the Nabataeans pursued and attacked his camp in the third watch, destroying almost all his 4,000 foot and 600 horse. A surprise attack on a camp rather than a set battle.

name: Eurymenae (first)
note: Alexander relieved his father besieged at Eurymenae; Diodorus does not state the winner explicitly but reports heavy losses for Cassander's army incl. its officers, and calls it defeated. Identification of Eurymenae uncertain.

name: Eurymenae (second)
commanders_b: Alexander and Teucer, sons of Alcetas II
note: With Deinias' reinforcements Cassander's army won a second battle; Eurymenae was then sacked.

name: Apollonia
place: before the walls of Apollonia, Illyria
note: The Apolloniates, who had expelled Cassander's garrison and called in allies (Illyrians of Glaucias), outnumbered and defeated Cassander in a long, hard battle.

name: Galaria
war: Agathocles' war with the Syracusan exiles
note: Exile army of c. 3,000 foot and 2,000 horse defeated; Galaria then taken.

name: Myus
note: Dawn surprise attack; Diodorus says Demetrius took the army 'without a battle', Plutarch that he routed it and took 7,000 prisoners. Counted as a battle by Wikipedia; borderline.

name: Himera River
place: Himera (Salso) river below Mount Ecnomus, near Licata
note: Agathocles stormed into the Carthaginian camp but was routed when reinforcements arrived; c. 7,000 Greeks killed. Also called the battle of Ecnomus.

name: Tigris
place: marshes by the Tigris, east of Babylonia (site unknown)
commanders_b: Nicanor (satrap of Media), Evagoras (satrap of Aria, killed)
note: Night attack from concealment in the marshes; Evagoras killed, most of Nicanor's army went over to Seleucus.

name: Libya (Aelymas)
note: Aelymas had allied with Agathocles and then deserted him.

name: Thates River
place: across the Thates river, Asian Bosporus (Kuban; site unknown)
commanders_b: Eumelus; Aripharnes, king of the Siraces
note: Satyrus' army was mostly Scythian (c. 20,000 foot, 10,000 horse); Eumelus' mostly the Siraces (Sarmatians) of Aripharnes. Satyrus was killed soon afterwards besieging Aripharnes' fortress (siege, not listed). Diodorus spells the river Thates (often 'Thatis').

name: Cilicia
war: Antigonus v Ptolemy (after the Peace of 311)
commanders_b: Leonides and other generals of Ptolemy
note: Diodorus says only that Demetrius 'defeated the generals of Ptolemy and recovered the cities'; no battle details.

name: Lake Maeotis (Eumelus v Prytanis)
place: Asian Bosporus near the isthmus by Lake Maeotis (site unknown)
note: Eumelus defeated his brother, shut him up in the isthmus by the Maeotis and forced his surrender.

name: Syracuse (Euryalus)
note: Field battle during the siege of Syracuse (311–309): the Syracusans attacked Hamilcar's army on its night march to Euryalus and routed it.

name: Herbessus
note: 'A bitter battle' with Agathocles' garrison, after which Herbessus was freed; may have been an assault on the town rather than a field battle.

name: Megara Hyblaea
place: off Megara (Hyblaea), at a shrine of Hera
note: Syracusans sailing out to escort grain ships lost 10 triremes to the Carthaginian blockading squadron.

name: Tunis
note: After the mutiny in his camp, Agathocles fell on the Carthaginians (who were expecting deserters) and inflicted heavy losses.

name: 25 Abu
sources: Polyaen. 4.9.1; cf. BCHP 3 (Chronicle of the Diadochi)
note: After an indecisive first day both sides rested; Seleucus' men attacked Antigonus' camp at dawn and won. The precise date is a modern reconstruction (Wikipedia 'Battle of the 25 of Abu'); Polyaenus gives no place or date.

name: Zuphones
place: territory of the Zuphones (Numidians), Libyan interior
note: The Numidians waited on the outcome and then plundered both baggage trains.

name: Hippou Acra
note: Agathocles beat the people of Hippou Acra (a Phoenician dependency of Carthage) in a naval battle and then stormed the city.

name: Akragas (first)
note: Xenodocus lost over 1,500 men and fled to Akragas.

name: Libya (Aeschrion)
note: Ambush of one of Archagathus' three divisions; Aeschrion and over 4,000 foot and 200 horse killed.

name: Libya (Eumachus)
place: Libyan interior, near a hill by a captured town (site unknown)
note: Feigned retreat; Eumachus' division (c. 8,000 foot) almost annihilated.

name: Syracuse (harbour)
note: Agathocles' 17 ships and 18 Etruscan ships surprised the 30-ship Carthaginian blockade, capturing 5 ships.

name: Akragas (second)
note: Second defeat of Xenodocus, who then withdrew to Gela.

name: Tunis
note: On his return to Africa Agathocles attacked the fortified Carthaginian camp and was driven back with c. 3,000 losses; he soon fled to Sicily.

name: Salamis (Cyprus)
note: Short battle before the siege; Menelaus lost c. 1,000 killed and 3,000 captured.

name: Salamis (Cyprus) (sea)
note: Decisive; led Antigonus and Demetrius to take the royal title.

name: Rhodes (harbour)
note: Harbour battle during the siege: three picked Rhodian ships rammed and overturned two of Demetrius' floating siege-engines; the admiral and one ship were captured when they pressed too far.

name: Rhodes (mole sortie)
note: Sortie battle: during a storm the Rhodians attacked the troops Demetrius had lodged on the mole; after a long fight over 400 surrendered.

name: Torgium
war: Agathocles' war with the Syracusan exiles
note: Agathocles (c. 5,000 foot, 800 horse) beat the exiles (c. 25,000 foot, 3,000 horse) when over 2,000 of them defected; thousands who surrendered were then massacred.

name: Thuriae (Sallentine)
commanders_a: M. Aemilius Paullus (consul) or C. Junius Bubulcus (dictator)
note: Livy: the Romans routed Cleonymus 'in one battle' and drove him to his ships; his annalists disagree on the Roman commander. Diodorus instead has native 'barbarians' (Messapians/Sallentines) defeat him in a night attack on his camp near Triopium, probably the same episode. Cleonymus by then was at odds with Taras and acting on his own.

name: Patavium
place: villages and river Meduacus near Patavium (Padua)
note: The Patavini routed his raiding parties and attacked his ships on the river; Cleonymus lost about four-fifths of his fleet. Known only from Livy, a native of Patavium.

name: Ipsus
sources: Diod. 21.1; Plut. Demetr. 28–30; Plut. Pyrrh. 4; App. Syr. 55; Just. 15.4.21–23

name: Cappadocia (Ariarathes v Amyntas)
commanders_a: Ariarathes II, with troops of Ardoates of Armenia
note: Diodorus says only that Ariarathes 'slew Amyntas the Macedonian general' and drove out the Macedonians while the Successors fought each other. Amyntas' master (probably Antigonus, possibly a post-Ipsus ruler) and the date are uncertain; Diodorus' Cappadocian genealogy is partly legendary.

name: Corcyra
note: Agathocles relieved Corcyra, besieged by Cassander by land and sea, and set fire to the whole Macedonian fleet.

name: Ethae
note: Night attack on Agathocles' camp while he besieged Ethae; 4,000 of his men killed and he withdrew to Syracuse.

name: Bithynia (Zipoetes v Lysimachus)
note: Memnon says Zipoetes killed one of Lysimachus' generals, drove another far from his land, and defeated Lysimachus himself; probably more than one engagement. Undated; often linked to Zipoetes' royal title (Bithynian era 297).

name: Mantinea
note: 'Antigonus I' = Demetrius before he took Macedon (later in 294).

name: Sparta
note: Second victory; 200 Spartans killed and 500 captured. Demetrius broke off to deal with Lysimachus and Ptolemy.

name: Aetolia (Pyrrhus v Pantauchus)
note: Demetrius had left Pantauchus with an army in Aetolia; the two kings' armies missed each other. Pyrrhus wounded Pantauchus in single combat and took 5,000 prisoners.

name: Hyblaeus River
place: near the Hyblaeus river (Dirillo near Camarina, or upper Irminio near Hybla Heraea)
note: River identification disputed (Wikipedia: Dirillo; Loeb: upper Hyrminius). Date from Wikipedia; Diodorus gives none (Hicetas ruled c. 288–279).

name: Cyrrhestica
place: Cyrrhestica, northern Syria, near the Amanus passes
note: Demetrius' night march failed; Seleucus' wing partly routed his army and Seleucus' personal appeal brought the rest over. Demetrius fled and surrendered soon after. Largely a defection; borderline as a battle.

name: Terias River
note: Date from Wikipedia; Diodorus gives none.

name: Taras
sources: App. Samn. 7.1; Dio fr. 39.4–5 (Zon. 8.2); Livy Per. 12; Oros. 4.1.1
note: The Tarentines attacked a Roman squadron of 10 ships entering the gulf, sinking 4 and capturing 1 (Appian); triggered the war.

name: Corupedium
sources: App. Syr. 62, 64; Just. 17.1.8–2.1; Memnon F 5.7; Paus. 1.10.5; Porph. FGrH 260 F 3.8

name: Heraclea
place: between Heraclea and Pandosia on the Siris, Lucania (near Policoro)
sources: Plut. Pyrrh. 16–17; Dion. Hal. 19.12; Flor. 1.13.7–8; Zon. 8.3; Oros. 4.1.8–15

name: Ptolemy Keraunos v Antigonus (sea)
place: Aegean, on Antigonus' attempted crossing to Macedon (site unknown)
note: Keraunos used Lysimachus' former fleet, in which the Heracleot ships (incl. the eight 'Leontophoros') fought best; Antigonus retreated to Boeotia. Site unknown.

name: Cirrha
note: Areus ravaged the sacred plain the Aetolians were cultivating; c. 500 Aetolians fell on the dispersed Spartans and routed them (Justin's figure of 9,000 killed is implausible). Close to an attack on plunderers; borderline.

name: Bithynia (Hermogenes)
war: Antiochus I v Bithynia and the Northern League
note: Antiochus' general Hermogenes was ambushed and killed with his whole army; probably the defeat of 'Antiochus son of Seleucus' credited to Zipoetes in Memnon F 12.5.

name: Asculum
commanders_b: P. Decius Mus, P. Sulpicius Saverrio
sources: Plut. Pyrrh. 21.5–10; Dion. Hal. 20.1–3; Zon. 8.5; Front. Strat. 2.3.21; Oros. 4.1.19–22
note: Two-day battle; the original 'Pyrrhic victory'. Some ancient accounts claimed a draw or Roman success.

name: Macedonia (death of Ptolemy Keraunos)
war: Celtic invasion of Macedon and Greece
note: Keraunos was thrown by his elephant, captured and beheaded; Diodorus says the whole Macedonian army was cut down. Site unknown.

name: Macedonia (Sosthenes v Bolgius)
war: Celtic invasion of Macedon and Greece
note: Sosthenes attacked the Gauls while they celebrated their victory and drove them out of Macedon.

name: Macedonia (Brennus v Sosthenes)
war: Celtic invasion of Macedon and Greece
note: The outnumbered Macedonians were beaten and shut themselves in their cities while Brennus plundered the country.

name: Thermopylae
note: The Greeks repulsed the frontal assaults with heavy Gallic losses, but Brennus turned the position by the Anopaea path and the Greek army was evacuated by the Athenian fleet. Wikipedia: Celtic victory at Thermopylae. 'Thebes' = the Boeotian contingent (10,000 hoplites).

name: Callium
note: After the Gauls sacked Callium, the Aetolian levy (incl. women and old men) and the Patraeans attacked them on their way back; fewer than half of the 40,800 reached Thermopylae. A running fight rather than one set battle.

name: Delphi
place: Delphi and the slopes of Parnassus
note: Ancient accounts dwell on divine intervention (earthquake, snowstorm, panic).

name: Spercheios River
note: Ambush of the retreating Gauls; Pausanias' claim that none got home is exaggerated.

name: Thynia
note: Heraclea lost many men, but Zipoetes withdrew when allied reinforcements arrived. 'Bithynia' here is Zipoetes' faction, not Nicomedes' kingdom (Nicomedes was Heraclea's ally).

name: Sicily (Pyrrhus v Mamertines)
note: Plutarch: Pyrrhus 'conquered them in battle and destroyed many of their strongholds'; no details.

name: Lysimachia
note: The Gauls attacked Antigonus' apparently abandoned camp and were cut down by his troops and sailors by the shore; the victory won him the Macedonian throne.

name: Strait of Messina
note: Carthaginians intercepted Pyrrhus' fleet on his return to Italy; he lost many ships but got across to Locri.

name: Bruttium (Mamertine attack on Pyrrhus)
place: rough country in Bruttium on the march toward Locri (site unknown)
note: Some 10,000 Mamertines who had crossed ahead attacked the march, killing two elephants and many of the rearguard; Pyrrhus, wounded, killed a Mamertine champion and the attackers drew off. Outcome judged indecisive.

name: Beneventum
sources: Plut. Pyrrh. 25; Dion. Hal. 20.11–12; Oros. 4.2.3–6; Flor. 1.13.11; Front. Strat. 2.2.1
note: Pyrrhus' night march failed; the sources are poor and some moderns see it as indecisive, but Pyrrhus then left Italy.

name: Elephant Victory
sources: Lucian, Zeuxis 8–11; App. Syr. 65; Suda s.v. Simonides
note: 16 elephants routed the Galatian cavalry and chariots. Date disputed: c. 275 commonly; Wörrle's c. 270–268 widely accepted. If dated 270–268 it falls just after this batch's range.

name: Aous
place: a narrow pass, conventionally near the Aous (Vjosa) river
note: Plutarch names only 'a narrow pass'; the Aous location is modern convention. Antigonus' Galatian rearguard was cut down, his elephants captured and his Macedonians went over to Pyrrhus.

name: Macedonia (Ptolemy son of Pyrrhus v Antigonus)
note: Antigonus, renewing the war with Gallic mercenaries, was 'utterly defeated' and fled with seven companions. Known only from Justin.

name: Cyamosorus River
note: Hieron deliberately let the Mamertines destroy his unruly mercenaries while he withdrew with the citizen troops. Date disputed.

name: Sparta
commanders_a: Acrotatus; Areus I (returning from Crete); Ameinias of Phocis
note: Two days of assaults on the trench and wagon barrier (with the women's famous part) beaten off; an assault on a city, included as the brief's 'fighting at the walls'.

name: Laconia (death of Ptolemy son of Pyrrhus)
place: difficult ground in Laconia on the march to Argos (site unknown)
note: Rearguard battle: Areus' picked troops routed the rearguard and killed Ptolemy; Pyrrhus' Molossian cavalry then cut down the Spartan force. Outcome debatable (Spartan ambush success v. Pyrrhus holding the field).

name: Argos
commanders_a: Antigonus II Gonatas, Halcyoneus; Areus I (Spartans)
note: Night entry into Argos ended in street fighting; Pyrrhus was struck by a roof tile thrown by a woman and killed.

name: Longanus River
war: Wars of Hiero II against the Mamertines
place: plain of Mylae by the river Longanus, NE Sicily
note: Date disputed: 269 (Hoyos, many chronologies) or 265/264; after it Hiero was acclaimed king. Hiero's earlier defeat at the Cyamosorus (Polyb. 1.9.4) is usually dated c. 274 and falls before this batch.

name: Megara
note: Trogus: Antigonus destroyed mutinous Gauls ('defectores Galli') at Megara; Justin tells of a Gallic army (Gallograeci) wiped out after killing their own families. Identifying the two accounts, and the site, is modern inference.

name: Corinth
note: Areus I was killed trying to break through the Macedonian blockade of Athens at the Isthmus; few details survive.

name: Messana
note: Polybius: Appius defeated the Syracusans besieging Messana and Hiero withdrew to Syracuse that night. Appius beat the Carthaginians the next day, a Rome v Carthage action not listed here. Philinus claimed Roman defeats, and some modern works call the Syracusan action inconclusive.

name: Derdia
war: War of Alexander II of Epirus against Macedon
commanders_a: Demetrius (later Demetrius II), son of Antigonus Gonatas
note: Only Eusebius names the site (and he miscalls Alexander 'Pyrrhus'); Justin says the young Demetrius raised an army, recovered Macedonia and drove Alexander out of Epirus. The site is unidentified, and the date is approximate.

name: Megalopolis
note: Pausanias calls the Spartan commander Acrotatus son of Cleomenes; Plutarch's Acrotatus son of Areus (Acrotatus II) is generally preferred. The date is approximate. 'Megalopolis' is a new entity name.

name: Cos
note: The date is much disputed: c. 262/261 at the end of the Chremonidean War, or 258/255 in the Second Syrian War. Antigonus dedicated his flagship at Delos afterwards.

name: Sardis
war: War of Eumenes I against Antiochus I
note: Known only from a single sentence in Strabo; it secured Pergamene independence.

name: Ephesus
date: c. 258 BCE (disputed: anywhere from c. 261 to 242)
note: Most scholars place it c. 259/258 in the Second Syrian War. Others put it in the Third Syrian War (c. 245–242) or treat it as a separate Rhodian–Ptolemaic conflict.

name: Mantinea
war: Spartan war against the Arcadians and Achaeans
commanders_a: Aratus of Sicyon; Lydiades and Leocydes of Megalopolis
commanders_b: Agis son of Eudamidas (killed, according to Pausanias)
note: Historicity doubted: known only from Pausanias, and Agis IV was in fact executed at Sparta in 241. Some accept a real battle c. 250/249 with a garbled Spartan commander. Included as uncertain.

name: Andros
note: 246/245 is generally accepted, but other dates (including a pre-250 date) have been proposed. Trogus' 'Oprona' is usually emended to Sophron.

name: Chaeronea
note: The side_b entity is the Boeotian League. About 1,000 Boeotians fell; Aratus' Achaean relief army arrived too late.

name: Syria (defeat of Seleucus II)
note: Justin says that Seleucus II made war on Ptolemy, was defeated and fled to Antioch. No site or detail survives; included as uncertain.

name: Pellene
note: Aratus attacked the Aetolians while they were scattered plundering the newly taken town and routed them, killing about 700.

name: Lydia
sources: Porphyry FGrH 260 F32.8 (Euseb. Chron., Armenian version)
note: Eusebius (who garbles Hierax's name as 'Antigonus') says Seleucus won in Lydia but could not take Sardis or Ephesus.

name: Ancyra
commanders_a: Antiochus Hierax; Mithridates II of Pontus
sources: Trogus Prol. 27; Justin 27.2.10–11; Porphyry FGrH 260 F32.8
note: Trogus credits the Gauls with the victory; Eusebius says it was against Mithridates and that about 20,000 of Seleucus' men fell. Seleucus barely escaped, and Asia Minor west of the Taurus was left to Hierax. Some scholars date it as late as c. 236/235.

name: Caicus Springs
place: near the sources of the river Caicus, Mysia
note: Fought against the Tolistoagii Galatians. After it Attalus took the title of king, and it was commemorated by the Gallic monuments at Pergamon.

name: Magnesia
sources: Porphyry FGrH 260 F32.8 (Euseb. Chron., Armenian version)
note: Highly uncertain. Eusebius says that Hierax, betrayed by his followers to 'the barbarians', escaped to Magnesia and won a battle there with Ptolemaic soldiers. The opponent is not named (the Galatians are assumed here) and neither is which Magnesia.

name: Chares River
war: Aratus' wars against the tyrants of Argos
note: Aratus' wing was winning, but he withdrew, so the Argives held the field and set up a trophy; usually judged indecisive. Some modern works call the river the Xerias.

name: Cleonae
war: Aratus' wars against the tyrants of Argos
place: Cleonae, with the pursuit to Mycenae
note: Aratus surprised Aristippus' army attacking Cleonae and routed it; Aristippus was killed in the flight near Mycenae.

name: Phylacia
place: Phylacia (site uncertain; perhaps Phylace in SE Arcadia)
note: The site is unidentified: Arcadia or Attica have both been proposed. False rumours of Aratus' death followed the defeat.

name: Medion
note: Relief battle during the Aetolian siege of Medion. Agron's Illyrians, bribed by Demetrius II, landed and routed the besiegers, helped by a sortie of the Medionians.

name: Phoenice
commanders_a: Teuta's commanders (Scerdilaidas commanded a second force)
note: The Illyrians took Phoenice when its Gallic mercenary garrison betrayed it. They then defeated the Epirote relief army camped by the river below the city.

name: Aphrodisium
war: Wars of Attalus I against Antiochus Hierax
place: by the Aphrodisium (sanctuary of Aphrodite) outside Pergamon
note: Fought against the Tolistoagii, the Tectosages and Antiochus Hierax (here counted as Seleucid Empire, for his breakaway Seleucid realm in Asia Minor). The order and dates of Attalus' victories are disputed.

name: Paxos
note: Fought to relieve besieged Corcyra. The Illyrian lembi, supported by 7 Acarnanian decked ships, beat 10 Achaean decked ships (Aetolian participation is minor or unclear): 4 quadriremes were captured and a quinquereme was sunk. Corcyra then surrendered.

name: Hellespontine Phrygia
war: Wars of Attalus I against Antiochus Hierax
note: Hierax was perhaps moving towards his father-in-law Ziaelas of Bithynia; the date is uncertain.

name: Coloe
war: Wars of Attalus I against Antiochus Hierax
place: near Lake Coloe (Marmara Gölü), north of Sardis
note: Eusebius says Hierax was defeated twice in Lydia in 229 and fought Attalus near Coloe; the second Lydian defeat (near Sardis?) is not separately located and not listed separately.

name: Macedonia (Dardanian invasion)
note: Trogus says that Demetrius II was routed by the Dardanians shortly before his death. The site, date and circumstances are unknown, and it is not certain that he died of the battle.

name: Harpasus
war: Wars of Attalus I against Antiochus Hierax
note: This final defeat drove Hierax out of Asia Minor.

name: Parthia (Arsaces I v Seleucus II)
war: Seleucid–Parthian war (eastern campaign of Seleucus II)
sources: Justin 41.4.9–10; cf. Strabo 11.8.8; Posidonius ap. Athen. 4.153a
note: Only Justin records the battle: Arsaces met Seleucus, who had come to punish the rebels, and won, and the Parthians kept the day as the start of their freedom. Strabo says Arsaces fled from Seleucus to the Apasiacae, and modern accounts (date usually c. 228) often have Arsaces retreat first and recover once Seleucus was called west. Posidonius' story that Seleucus II was captured probably confuses him with Demetrius II. Date, site and the battle's character are all uncertain; coordinates are a placeholder in the Parthian heartland (Astauene).

name: Mesopotamia (rout of Antiochus Hierax)
note: Trogus: 'Antiochus in Mesopotamia a Callinico fugatus'. No details survive, the date is uncertain, and it is not certain that this was a pitched battle.

name: Mount Lycaeum
note: Cleomenes routed the Achaean army, which had been marching to attack Elis.

name: Ladoceia
note: Lydiades' cavalry charged against Aratus' orders and was cut up in broken ground; the Achaean army was then routed.

name: Orchomenus
note: A minor action: about 300 Spartans were killed and Megistonous was taken.

name: Dyme
place: Hecatombaeum, territory of Dyme, W Achaea
note: Also called Hecatombaeum. The crushing defeat drove the Achaeans to seek Antigonus Doson's help.

name: Lechaeum
place: Cleomenes' fortified line across the Isthmus, at Lechaeum
note: An assault on a fortified line, not a pitched battle: Antigonus tried to force a passage at Lechaeum and was repulsed with loss. He was soon able to turn the line when Argos revolted. Included as uncertain.

name: Lysias and the generals of Seleucus
place: western Asia Minor (site lost from the inscription)
commanders_b: Lysias and the generals of Seleucus (II or III)
note: Known only from Attalid victory dedications. The place name is lost and the date is uncertain: against Seleucus II's generals after Hierax's flight, or Seleucus III's c. 224/223.

name: Sellasia
place: pass of Sellasia (hills Evas and Olympus), N Laconia
commanders_a: Antigonus III Doson; Philopoemen (cavalry); Demetrius of Pharos
note: Thebes stands for the Boeotian contingent. The Achaean contingent included the Megalopolitans.

name: Macedonia (Illyrian invasion)
note: Doson hurried back from Sellasia to meet an Illyrian (probably Dardanian) invasion and beat it in a pitched battle. He burst a blood vessel while shouting during the fighting and died soon after.

name: Brochi
war: Prelude to the Fourth Syrian War
place: the fortified pass of Gerrha and Brochi in the Marsyas valley (Beqaa)
note: An assault on fortified lines blocking the pass. Antiochus failed to force them, lost more men than the defenders, and gave up the invasion of Coele-Syria. The sites of Gerrha and Brochi are only approximately identified. Included as uncertain.

name: Tigris
place: east bank of the Tigris, near Seleucia on the Tigris
note: Molon feigned retreat and then fell at dawn on Xenoetas' camp while the troops were drunk and asleep. The royal army was destroyed, many drowning in the river, and Molon went on to take Seleucia.

name: Apollonia
note: Molon's left wing went over to the king as the armies closed, and Molon killed himself. The site of Apollonia (somewhere in the Diyala basin) is not securely identified.

name: Dyme
place: territory of Dyme, Pharae and Tritaea, W Achaea
note: A minor action: Euripidas, raiding from Elis, defeated the local Achaean levies under Miccus. Included as an obscure battle.

name: Apelaurum
place: Mount Apelaurum near Stymphalus, NE Arcadia
note: Euripidas' force (2 Elean companies, pirates and mercenaries, about 2,200 men and 100 horse) ran into Philip's army on the march; about 1,200 were captured. Also called Stymphalus. Philip had set out about the winter solstice, so the clash may fall in Dec. 219 or early 218.

name: Thermum
place: on Philip's retreat route from Thermum, Aetolia
note: A rearguard action rather than a pitched battle, included as uncertain. Aetolians attacking the rear of Philip's army after the sack of Thermum were ambushed by his Illyrian troops and routed.

name: Menelaion
place: heights of the Menelaion, across the Eurotas from Sparta
commanders_a: Philip V; Demetrius of Pharos; Aratus
note: Philip dislodged Lycurgus' Spartans from the heights commanding his line of retreat.

name: Porphyreon
place: coastal defile between Berytus and Sidon near Porphyreon (Platanus pass)
commanders_a: Antiochus III; Theodotus the Aetolian; Menedemus
note: Theodotus turned Nicolaus' position from the mountain side and the Ptolemaic line broke, with about 2,000 killed and 2,000 captured. A simultaneous sea battle offshore is listed separately.

name: Porphyreon (sea)
place: off Porphyreon, between Berytus and Sidon
note: The fleets fought evenly. Perigenes withdrew to Sidon once the Ptolemaic army was beaten on land.

name: Pednelissus
note: Relief battle during the Selgian siege of Pednelissus. Garsyeris forced the passes, defeated the Selgians before the town and raised the siege; Achaeus then besieged Selge. Achaeus was a Seleucid usurper (king from 220), counted here as Seleucid Empire. Selge claimed Spartan origin but is treated as Pisidian ('Pisidians' is a new entity name). Details are from Polybius' fuller narrative and not re-verified.

name: Leontion
note: The enemy lost about 400 killed and 200 captured. A follow-up Achaean raid into Elis (200 killed, 80 taken) is not listed separately.

name: Raphia
place: south of Raphia (Rafah), between Gaza and Egypt
commanders_a: Ptolemy IV; Sosibius; Echecrates; Phoxidas; Andromachus; Ptolemy son of Thraseas
commanders_b: Antiochus III; Theodotus the Aetolian; Nicarchus; Theodotus Hemiolius

name: Arisba
note: Prusias destroyed the Aegosages, Gauls whom Attalus I had brought over, who were holding Arisba. The men fell in battle and most of the women and children in the camp were massacred.

name: Apollonia (relief)
place: Philip's siege camp before Apollonia, Illyria (Aous valley)
commanders_a: Q. Naevius Crista (for M. Valerius Laevinus)
note: A night attack on the besiegers' camp. Philip fled half-dressed to his ships and burnt them. The account is Livy's alone and its scale is often doubted.

name: Acrillae
note: Marcellus caught the Syracusan field army (about 10,000 foot and 500 horse) while it was pitching camp and routed it. Hippocrates escaped with the cavalry to Acrae and then joined Himilco.

name: Syracuse (relief battle)
place: Roman siege lines outside Syracuse (Achradina and the old camp)
commanders_a: M. Claudius Marcellus; T. Quinctius Crispinus
commanders_b: Himilco and Hippocrates (relief army); Epicydes (sortie from Achradina)
note: A combined assault by the Carthaginian relief army on the Roman camp and a sortie by the Syracusans under Epicydes; both were repulsed. It was a battle within the siege, included as uncertain. The siege itself is excluded.

name: Echinus (relief)
place: Philip's siege lines before Echinus, Phthiotis
note: A combined Roman–Aetolian attempt to relieve Echinus was beaten off at Philip's lines, and the town then surrendered. The siege itself is excluded.

name: Larisus River
place: river Larisus, on the Achaean–Elean border
note: Mainly a cavalry battle; Philopoemen killed Damophantus in single combat.

name: Sapriportis
place: off Sapriportis, about 15 Roman miles from Tarentum
note: The Tarentine fleet (Taras was then allied to Hannibal) defeated a Roman squadron bringing supplies to the besieged citadel. The site of Sapriportis is unidentified.

name: Lamia (first)
note: The first of two battles near Lamia in the same campaign. Pyrrhias had Attalus' auxiliaries and 1,000 Romans sent by Sulpicius.

name: Lamia (second)
note: The second of two battles near Lamia; afterwards the Aetolians and their allies stayed inside the walls.

name: Elis
note: Philip unexpectedly met Sulpicius' 4,000 Romans landed to reinforce Elis. His horse was killed and he barely escaped, and he withdrew; the next day he took the fort of Phyricus with 4,000 prisoners. Judgements range from inconclusive to a Macedonian repulse.

name: Mount Labus
place: pass over Mount Labus (Elburz range), between Hecatompylos and Hyrcania
commanders_a: Antiochus III, Diogenes, Polyxenidas of Rhodes, Nicomedes of Cos, Nicolaus the Aetolian
commanders_b: Arsaces II (presence at the pass not stated by Polybius)
note: The light troops took the heights over several days of fighting; the barbarians holding the pass were outflanked and routed, and most fled to Sirynx, which was then besieged (the siege is excluded). Bar-Kochva puts the route from Shahrud over the Chalchanlyan Pass toward Astrabad/Gorgan, so the coordinates are approximate. Justin's statement that Arsaces II fought Antiochus 'with remarkable courage' with 100,000 foot and 20,000 horse before becoming his ally may refer to this campaign; no separate battle is located.

name: Arius
war: Eastern anabasis of Antiochus III (Bactrian campaign)
place: ford of the river Arius (Hari Rud), on the road from Aria into Bactria
commanders_b: cavalry of Euthydemus I (Euthydemus himself was at 'Tapuria'/Guriana)
note: A cavalry battle: Antiochus forced the ford at night, then routed the 10,000 Bactrian horse at dawn; he was wounded in the mouth and his horse was killed. Euthydemus fell back to Zariaspa/Bactra, and the two-year siege of Bactra that followed (excluded) ended in a negotiated peace (206). The exact ford is unknown, somewhere on the Hari Rud in the Herat region or further downstream toward Sarakhs. A Greek v Greek battle.

name: Mantinea
note: Philopoemen killed Machanidas with his own hand.

name: Lade
war: Cretan War / Philip V's Aegean campaign
place: strait between the island of Lade and Miletus
note: Rhodian historians claimed a victory; Polybius rejects this, since two Rhodian quinqueremes were captured and the fleet withdrew to Myndus and Cos. Whether Lade came before or after Chios is disputed (Walbank: before).

name: Chios
war: Cretan War / Philip V's Aegean campaign
place: strait between Chios and the Erythraean peninsula (near Cape Argennum)
note: Philip lost far more ships and men, but claimed victory: he anchored among the wrecks at Argennum and had captured Attalus' flagship after driving Attalus ashore. Polybius and modern scholars judge it a Pergamene–Rhodian success. Byzantine ships were in the allied fleet.

name: Athens (Dipylon)
note: Athenian sally (with Attalid troops and mercenaries) routed back into the city by Philip's surprise attack; Philip's later assaults on Athens, Piraeus and Eleusis failed (not counted).

name: Panium
place: near Paneas (Banias), at the sources of the Jordan
sources: Polyb. 16.18–19, 16.39.3; Porphyry FGrH 260 F46 (Jerome, In Dan. 11.15); Jos. AJ 12.132
note: Exact field disputed: the plain between Paneas and Tel Dan (Bar-Kochva) is the usual placement; the site lies at the edge of the Golan Heights.

name: Ottolobus
place: Ottolobus, near Athacus in Lyncestis (Upper Macedonia)
note: Cavalry clashes followed by Philip's attack on Roman foragers, which was beaten off with Philip nearly captured; also called the fighting at Athacus. Exact site in the Lyncus/Pelagonia plain unknown (Greece–North Macedonia border area).

name: Eordaea Pass
place: fortified pass from Lyncus into Eordaea
note: Romans stormed Philip's field fortifications blocking the pass (often identified with the Kirli Derven pass). Included as a small but real engagement.

name: Pharcadon
note: Philip surprised the Aetolian and Athamanian army plundering Thessaly and routed it. Some date it to 200.

name: Upper Macedonia (Athenagoras v Dardanians)
place: Upper Macedonia, on the Dardanians' line of retreat
note: Athenagoras attacked the Dardanians retreating with booty; they turned and fought a pitched action, then withdrew in good order with few losses. Sometimes counted as a Macedonian success.

name: Aous
note: Flamininus turned Philip's position with the help of a shepherd guide supplied by the Epirote Charops. Some locate the narrows near Konitsa (Greece) instead.

name: Nemea River
place: by the Nemea river, between Corinthian and Sicyonian territory
note: Achaean surprise attack on Philip's Corinth garrison army while it was dispersed plundering; Macedonians routed.

name: Alabanda
note: Rhodian army (with Achaean and mercenary troops) defeated Philip's Carian garrison forces and recovered the Peraea; Stratonicea held out.

name: Cynoscephalae
note: Aetolians supplied c. 6,000 foot and 400 horse and claimed a large share of the credit, hence listed as principal.

name: Stobi
note: Philip, just after Cynoscephalae, defeated an invading Dardanian army with a hastily raised levy.

name: Gytheum
note: Achaean squadron defeated while trying to relieve besieged Gytheum; Philopoemen's old flagship broke up at the first ramming.

name: Mount Barbosthenes
note: Nabis ambushed the Achaean column in a defile but was routed; mountain not securely identified (about 10 Roman miles from Sparta).

name: Thermopylae
place: pass of Thermopylae and the heights of Callidromus
commanders_a: M'. Acilius Glabrio, M. Porcius Cato, L. Valerius Flaccus
sources: Livy 36.15–19; App. Syr. 17–20; Plut. Cat. Mai. 13–14
note: The Aetolians held the mountain forts (Callidromus, Teichius); Cato's capture of them decided the battle, hence Aetolians listed as principal.

name: Corycus
place: off Cape Corycus, Erythraean peninsula, Ionia
note: Pergamene squadron of c. 50 ships (24 decked) was a major part of the allied fleet; a few Carthaginian ships also present.

name: Panormus
note: Polyxenidas trapped the Rhodian fleet by a feigned offer of treachery; Pausistratus killed and most of his ships lost. Exact site of the Samian Panormus uncertain.

name: Pergamon (sortie)
place: plain below Pergamon during Seleucus' siege
note: Sortie battle: 1,000 Achaean foot and 100 horse under Diophanes routed the besieging Seleucid troops, leading Seleucus to raise the siege.

name: Side
place: off Side, near the mouth of the Eurymedon, Pamphylia
note: Also called the battle of the Eurymedon; Hannibal's only naval battle.

name: Myonessus
place: between Myonnesus and the Corycus peninsula, Ionia
note: The Rhodian squadron with its fire-pots played a decisive role.

name: Magnesia
place: plain near Magnesia ad Sipylum, Lydia
commanders_a: L. Cornelius Scipio, Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, Eumenes II
note: Eumenes' cavalry charge was decisive. Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia sent 2,000 men and Galatians served in large numbers on the Seleucid side.

name: Elymais (death of Antiochus III)
note: Borderline: Antiochus' night attempt to plunder the temple was met by the local population, who killed him 'with his whole army' (Justin). More an armed rising against a temple raid than a set battle. Temple site unknown; placed generically in the Elymaean highlands.

name: Thebaid (defeat of Chaonnophris)
note: Known from a documentary (hieroglyphic/demotic) decree, not a literary historian; the rebel army included Nubian (Kushite) troops. Site unknown, placed at Thebes.

name: Lypedron
sources: OGIS 298; Telmessus decree honouring Eumenes II (victory over Prusias and Ortiagon)
note: Known only from Attalid inscriptions (dedication 'from the battle against the Bithynians and Galatians at the Lypedron'); site unknown.

name: Propontis (Hannibal v Eumenes)
note: Hannibal's fleet won by hurling pots of snakes onto the Pergamene ships and targeting Eumenes' flagship. Location not given in the sources.

name: Corone
note: Cavalry action in which Philopoemen was unhorsed, captured and later poisoned at Messene. Messene surrendered to Lycortas the next year. Dated 183 or 182.

name: Callinicus
place: hill of Callinicus near Larissa, Thessaly
commanders_b: P. Licinius Crassus, Eumenes II, Attalus
note: Mainly a cavalry and light-troop battle; the Romans lost over 2,000 and withdrew across the Peneus, but Perseus did not exploit it (some modern accounts call it inconclusive).

name: Phalanna
note: Perseus' attack on Roman foragers was turned back by a Roman counter-attack; Livy gives two versions, one of them a larger battle.

name: Uscana (sortie)
note: Sortie battle: the garrison sallied and routed Claudius' army (only about 1,000 escaped, per Livy).

name: Dardania
note: Perseus' punitive campaign against the Dardanians, said to have killed 10,000; uncertain whether one pitched battle. Site region could equally lie in Kosovo/Serbia.

name: Pelusium–Mount Casius
place: between Pelusium and Mount Casius, NE Egypt
commanders_b: generals of Ptolemy VI (regime of Eulaeus and Lenaeus)
sources: Porphyry FGrH 260 F49a (Jerome, In Dan. 11.21–24); Diod. 30.14–18; 1 Macc 1.16–19
note: Date disputed (Nov. 170 vs 169). Followed by the surrender of Pelusium and Antiochus' advance to Memphis.

name: Elpeus
place: dry bed of the river Elpeus (Enipeas), Pieria
note: Two days of Roman attacks on Perseus' fortified line, repulsed with Roman losses; indecisive. Paullus then turned the position via Pythium.

name: Pythium
place: pass near Pythium, northern slopes of Mount Olympus
note: Nasica's flanking column overcame the Macedonian force guarding the pass, forcing Perseus back to Pydna.

name: Pydna
date: 168 BCE (22 June, the day after the lunar eclipse)
place: plain south of Pydna, near Katerini
note: End of the Antigonid kingdom. Cotys' Odrysian Thracians fought for Perseus.

name: Cyprus
note: Livy says Antiochus' fleet had beaten the Egyptian ships in a naval battle before the Romans sent it home after Eleusis; Polybius says only that Ptolemy's generals on Cyprus had been defeated in battle. Uncertain whether the decisive action was at sea or on land.

name: Ascent of Lebonah
place: on the Samaria–Jerusalem road (Lebonah or Wadi Haramiya)
note: Also called Battle of Wadi Haramia / Nahal el-Haramiah. Site not certain: near Lebonah (Avi-Yonah) or Wadi el-Haramiya north of Silwad.

name: Eumenes II v Galatians
note: Eumenes' victory ending the Galatian war that began with Galatian attacks in 168; no battle details or site recorded.

name: Beth Horon
place: ascent of Beth Horon, NW of Jerusalem

name: Emmaus
commanders_b: Gorgias, Nicanor, Ptolemy son of Dorymenes

name: Eleusis (Petosarapis)
note: Dionysius, a courtier, gathered c. 4,000 mutinous soldiers at Eleusis and was defeated by the king; he escaped by swimming the river and raised a native rising in the chora. Treated here as a native/rebel side; could be classed as Ptolemaic civil strife. Exact battle site not stated.

name: Beth Zur
note: 2 Macc presents the outcome as followed by negotiations; Lysias withdrew and Judas reoccupied the Temple.

name: Elymais (Antiochus IV repulsed)
note: Borderline: Polybius says the local tribes would not allow the temple robbery; 1 Macc says the inhabitants 'rose against him in battle' and he fled; 2 Macc places it at 'Persepolis' with his men routed. Antiochus died soon after at Tabae/Gabae.

name: Dathema (relief)
note: Relief battle: Judas attacked Timotheus' army besieging the Jews in Dathema at dawn and routed it. Timotheus is usually taken as a Seleucid commander leading garrison troops, locals and hired Arabs. Dathema unidentified (Ramtha? Dameh?).

name: Raphon
place: Raphon (Raphana?), across a stream near Carnaim, Hauran
note: Timotheus' force included hired Arabs; its Seleucid character rests on Timotheus being a royal officer (2 Macc). Followed by the burning of Carnaim.

name: Jamnia
note: About 2,000 Jews killed.

name: Marisa
note: Known mainly from 2 Macc (Gorgias wounded, his men routed and fleeing to Marisa); 1 Macc mentions only Jewish losses near Marisa. Historicity and outcome somewhat uncertain.

name: Beth Zechariah
place: Beth Zechariah, between Bethlehem and Beth Zur
note: Seleucid war elephants; Eleazar killed stabbing an elephant.

name: Cyrenaica (revolt against Ptolemy VIII)
place: Marmarica / eastern Cyrenaica, six days' march west of the Great Catabathmus (site unknown)
commanders_b: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II (Physcon); Mochyrinus (commanding the coasting force)
note: While Ptolemy VIII was in Libya (landed at Apis) after his appeal to Rome, the Cyrenaeans revolted, joined by Ptolemy Sympetesis, the governor he had left in charge. Ptolemy forced the pass of the Great Catabathmus (held by Libyans and Cyrenaeans, who abandoned it when he sent half his force round by sea) and took Tetrapyrgia, then after six days' march found the Cyrenaeans (8,000 foot, 500 horse) encamped; they offered battle at once and he was defeated. He recovered Cyrene by the end of 162, by unknown means. Site unknown; coordinates are a placeholder near Tobruk (Antipyrgos). Cyrene v its own Ptolemaic king, coded as Cyrene v Ptolemaic Egypt.

name: Capharsalama
note: Outcome disputed: 1 Macc has c. 500 of Nicanor's men fall and the rest flee to the City of David (the Akra); Josephus says Nicanor beat Judas. Small engagement.

name: Adasa
place: Adasa, near Beth Horon / north of Jerusalem
note: Celebrated as Nicanor's Day.

name: Elasa
note: Site identification (Khirbet Il'asa?) uncertain.

name: Jordan (Bacchides v Jonathan)
place: banks and marshes of the lower Jordan
note: Indecisive: Bacchides trapped Jonathan against the river on the Sabbath and lost c. 1,000 men (Josephus: 2,000); Jonathan's men escaped by swimming the Jordan.

name: Eucratides v Demetrius (sorties)
date: c. 170–150 BCE (undated; between Eucratides' accession c. 171 and his Indian conquest before his death c. 145)
war: Wars of Eucratides I (against the Euthydemids)
place: unnamed stronghold where Eucratides was besieged, probably in Bactria
note: Justin: when besieged by Demetrius, king of the Indians, Eucratides used his 300 men in repeated sorties to defeat 60,000 of the enemy, was freed in the fifth month (four in some manuscripts) and then brought India under his rule. Treated here as a sortie battle; the figures are rhetorical. It is disputed which Demetrius this was (I or II, or another Euthydemid). Coded as a civil war because Eucratides was a usurper fighting the Euthydemid dynasty of the same Bactrian–Indian realm. The site is unknown; the coordinates are Bactra, as a regional placeholder.

name: Bethbasi (sortie)
place: Bethbasi (Beth Hogla), in the Judean wilderness near Tekoa
note: Battle during a siege: Simon sallied, burned the siege engines and fought Bacchides, who 'was crushed', while Jonathan struck from outside. Led to the peace with Bacchides.

name: Prusias II v Attalus II
place: Pergamene territory, before Prusias' advance on Pergamon (site unknown)
note: Polybius refers to Prusias' 'victory over Attalus' before he besieged Pergamon; Appian describes Attalus fleeing at Prusias' approach, so a pitched battle is uncertain.

name: Sindhu
date: c. 160–150 BCE (late in the reign of Pushyamitra Shunga, c. 185–149 BCE)
place: south bank of the river Sindhu (probably the Kali Sindh, Hadoti region, Rajasthan)
sources: Kalidasa, Malavikagnimitra act 5 (Pushyamitra's letter); cf. Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva (Pushyamitra's two horse sacrifices)
note: Indians = the Shunga empire. The only source is a play by Kalidasa (c. 4th–5th c. CE): Yavana horsemen seized Pushyamitra's sacrificial horse on the south bank of the Sindhu, and in a 'great fight' between the two forces Vasumitra won and recovered the horse. Historicity, scale (possibly a large skirmish) and date are uncertain. The Sindhu is identified variously with the Kali Sindh (Chambal tributary), the Sindh (Yamuna tributary) or the Indus (Pakistan); the coordinates are on the Kali Sindh, so the location is regional only.

name: Rhodian–Cretan sea battle
note: Cretan cities (not individually named) defeated a Rhodian fleet; location and details lost with the fragmentary sources.

name: Syria (Demetrius I v Balas)
date: c. 152–151 BCE (before the decisive battle of 150)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Alexander Balas v Demetrius I)
place: Syria/Phoenicia (site unknown; Balas' base was Ptolemais)
sources: Justin 35.1.10 ('primo proelio hostem fugavit'); cf. 1 Macc 10.2; Jos. AJ 13.35–36
note: Justin says Demetrius routed the enemy in the first battle, and only when the kings backing Balas (Ptolemy VI, Attalus II, Ariarathes V) renewed the war was he defeated and killed (150). Smith's Dictionary dates this first defeat of Balas to 152. Josephus and 1 Macc describe only the final battle (in which Demetrius' left wing at first put its opponents to flight), so some may read Justin's 'first battle' as an earlier phase of that battle; included with that caveat. Site unknown; coordinates are a placeholder at Ptolemais.

name: Syria (Balas v Demetrius I)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Alexander Balas v Demetrius I)
place: northern Syria, probably near Antioch (site unknown)
note: Balas was backed by Ptolemy VI, Attalus II, Ariarathes V and Jonathan; whether their contingents fought here is unclear. Demetrius' horse bogged in a marsh and he was killed. Site unknown.

name: Odomantice
commanders_b: commanders of the eastern Macedonian republic
note: Andriscus, with Thracian troops of Teres and Barsabas, defeated the levy of the eastern Macedonian republic; details and exact date uncertain.

name: Strymon
note: Second victory over the republican levies, after which Andriscus was accepted as king of Macedon.

name: Thessaly (Scipio Nasica)
note: Uncertain whether a single battle: Scipio Nasica, with Achaean and Thessalian forces, drove Andriscus' army back out of Thessaly.

name: Thessaly (Juventius' defeat)
sources: Polyb. 36.17; Diod. 32.9a; Livy Per. 50; Liv. Oxy. Epit. 50; Flor. 1.30.4–5; Eutrop. 4.13; Zonar. 9.28
note: The praetor P. Juventius Thalna was killed and his legion almost destroyed ('in Thessalia exercitus caesus'). Dated 149 (CAH) or 148.

name: Pydna
sources: Diod. 32.9b, 32.15.7; Livy Per. 50; Vell. 1.11; Paus. 7.13.1; Eutrop. 4.13; Zonar. 9.28
note: Andriscus won an initial cavalry fight, but after the defection of Telestes with part of the cavalry Metellus routed him.

name: Thrace (Andriscus' last battle)
note: Andriscus raised new forces in Thrace and was defeated again by Metellus, then handed over by the Thracian dynast Byzes. Site (and modern country) unknown.

name: Sparta
note: The Spartans who came out to fight were routed with heavy loss, but Damocritus did not press the attack on the city and was fined.

name: Azotus
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Jonathan for Alexander Balas)
commanders_b: Apollonius (governor of Coele-Syria for Demetrius II)
note: Jonathan fought as Alexander Balas' strategos against the forces of Demetrius II; afterwards he burned Azotus and its temple of Dagon.

name: Scarpheia
note: Critolaus, retreating from the siege of Heraclea, was overtaken and defeated; he disappeared (drowned in the marshes or poisoned). The Thebans (Boeotarch Pytheas) had pledged support to the Achaeans.

name: Chaeronea
note: Metellus caught and destroyed about 1,000 picked Arcadian troops of the League retreating from Elatea; perhaps more a rout than a battle.

name: Corinth (Leucopetra)
place: Leucopetra on the Isthmus, outside Corinth
note: Preceded by a successful Achaean night attack on Roman outposts. Mummius had Attalid troops and Cretan archers. Corinth was then sacked and destroyed.

name: Oenoparas
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Demetrius II and Ptolemy VI v Alexander Balas)
note: Ptolemy VI died of his wounds days later; Balas fled to Arabia and was murdered. Identification of the Oenoparas (Afrin or a stream near Gephyra) uncertain.

name: Antioch (uprising)
commanders_a: Demetrius II; 3,000 Jewish troops sent by Jonathan
note: Borderline (urban fighting): the citizens besieged Demetrius in his palace; the Jewish contingent, credited by 1 Macc with the victory, fought through the city and burned it.

name: Syria (Tryphon v Demetrius II)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Tryphon and Antiochus VI v Demetrius II)
place: northern Syria, between Chalcis and Antioch (site unknown)
note: Tryphon took Demetrius' elephants and then Apamea and Antioch. Site not recorded.

name: Hazor
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Jonathan for Antiochus VI)
place: plain of Hazor, Upper Galilee; pursuit to Kedesh
commanders_a: Jonathan; Mattathias son of Absalom, Judas son of Chalphi
note: Jonathan's army was first routed by an ambush, then rallied and defeated the enemy.

name: Ptolemais (Sarpedon)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Tryphon v Demetrius II)
note: Posidonius: Sarpedon was beaten and Tryphon's men, pursuing along the shore, were drowned by a sudden sea-wave. Strabo instead has the Ptolemaeans routed by Sarpedon and the fugitives drowned. Date and winner therefore uncertain.

name: Media (capture of Demetrius II)
sources: Justin 36.1.4–6, 38.9.2; 1 Macc 14.1–3; Jos. AJ 13.184–186; App. Syr. 67; Astronomical Diary -137 A
note: Demetrius had won several earlier engagements (Justin) before being defeated, by a ruse, and captured. Allies per Justin.

name: Syria (Antiochus VII v Tryphon)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Antiochus VII v Tryphon)
note: Josephus: Antiochus beat Tryphon in battle and drove him from Upper Syria into Phoenicia and to Dor (then besieged). 1 Macc mentions only Tryphon's flight. Site unknown.

name: Kedron
place: coastal plain near Modiin and Kedron (Gedera?), pursuit to Azotus
commanders_a: Judas and John (Hyrcanus), sons of Simon
note: Also called the battle of Modiin; Josephus has the aged Simon himself take part. Exact site uncertain.

name: Cyme
note: The Ephesian fleet defeated Aristonicus, who was driven from the coast into the interior.

name: Leucae
place: near Leucae, Ionia (between Smyrna and Phocaea)
note: The consul Crassus was defeated and killed while campaigning to retake Leucae; battle site not recorded precisely. Dated 131 or 130.

name: Stratonicea (Caicus)
place: probably near Stratonicea on the Caicus, Mysia/Lydia
note: Perperna defeated Aristonicus 'at the first encounter' and then starved him out in Stratonicea (siege not counted); battle site disputed.

name: Lycus (Great Zab)
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus FGrH 90 F92 ap. Jos. AJ 13.250–252; Justin 38.10.6; Diod. 34/35.15–16
note: One of the three victories Justin credits to Antiochus in 130; the other two are unnamed. Crossing point on the Great Zab unknown.

name: Egypt (Hegelochus v Marsyas)
war: Ptolemaic civil war (Ptolemy VIII v Cleopatra II)
note: Hegelochus took Marsyas, general of the Alexandrians, alive and destroyed his army; Ptolemy pardoned him. Date and site not given.

name: Ecbatana
note: Antiochus' army was dispersed in winter quarters among rebellious Median towns; he fell attacking the Parthian king with the troops at hand. Exact site unknown ('Battle of Ecbatana' is a modern label).

name: Damascus
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Alexander II Zabinas v Demetrius II)
note: Zabinas was sent by Ptolemy VIII 'with an army' (Josephus). Placement near Damascus follows modern accounts (Ehling); Josephus gives no site. Demetrius fled to Ptolemais and was killed at Tyre.

name: Syria (Grypus v Zabinas)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Antiochus VIII v Alexander II Zabinas)
note: Grypus had Egyptian support from Ptolemy VIII. Diodorus says Zabinas avoided battle and fled with temple treasure; Justin and Josephus report a defeat. Zabinas was captured and executed.

name: Syria (Grypus v Cyzicenus)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Antiochus VIII v Antiochus IX)
note: Cyzicenus defeated and fled; Grypus took Antioch and Tryphaena had Cleopatra IV killed. Only source Justin; site unknown.

name: Syria (Cyzicenus v Grypus)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Antiochus IX v Antiochus VIII)
note: Cyzicenus captured and executed Tryphaena; Grypus retreated (to Aspendus per some reconstructions). Only source Justin; site unknown.

name: Chersonesus
note: Diophantus, sent by Mithridates VI to aid Chersonesus, routed Palacus' Scythians who attacked him with a large army; chronology of the campaigns (c. 110–107) disputed.

name: Crimea (Roxolani)
note: Strabo: 6,000 under Diophantus defeated about 50,000 Roxolani who had come to help Palacus; the decree calls them Rheuxinali.

name: Samaria (relief battle)
commanders_a: Aristobulus and Antigonus, sons of John Hyrcanus
note: Relief battle during Hyrcanus' siege of Samaria: Cyzicenus came to help the city, was beaten and pursued to Scythopolis.

name: Cimmerian Bosporus
place: on the frozen Strait of Kerch
note: Cavalry battle fought on the ice of the strait; Strabo says only 'the barbarians' (probably Scythians or Maeotians). Date uncertain, probably soon after Diophantus' campaigns.

name: Cimmerian Bosporus (sea)
note: Naval victory at the same place as the winter battle on the ice; opponents 'the barbarians'.

name: Judea (Callimander)
note: Antiochus IX, reinforced by 6,000 men from Ptolemy IX, left Callimander and Epicrates in command; Callimander attacked rashly and was routed and killed. Minor; whether Ptolemaic troops were present is unclear.

name: Ptolemais
war: War of the Sceptres (Jannaeus' coastal campaign)
note: Jannaeus beat the Ptolemaeans in battle and then besieged the city, which called in Ptolemy IX. Ptolemais counted as a Hellenistic polis (Greek side) here; drop if Levantine poleis are not to count.

name: Asophon
note: Ptolemy IX was then ruling only Cyprus (in conflict with Cleopatra III and Ptolemy X). Josephus gives 30,000 Jewish dead (Timagenes 50,000). Asophon usually identified with Zaphon (Tell es-Sa'idiyeh or Tell el-Qos), east of the Jordan.

name: Amathus
note: After Jannaeus took Amathus, Theodorus fell on the Jews unexpectedly, killed 10,000 and took the baggage. Theodorus' father Zeno Cotylas was tyrant of Philadelphia (AJ 13.235); counted as a Hellenistic tyranny here, which is debatable.

name: Gaza (sortie)
note: Night sortie by 2,000 mercenaries and 10,000 citizens; successful in the dark, but at daybreak the Jews rallied and killed c. 1,000 Gazaeans. Gaza fell after a year's siege. Gaza counted as a Hellenistic polis here (debatable).

name: Cappadocia (Sulla)
note: Sulla killed many Cappadocians of Gordius' pro-Pontic regime and more Armenians who came to help them, and installed Ariobarzanes I. Date of Sulla's mission disputed (96 or 92).

name: Syria (Seleucus VI v Antiochus IX)
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Seleucus VI v Antiochus IX)
sources: Jos. AJ 13.366; App. Syr. 69; Euseb. Chron. (Porphyry FGrH 260 F32)
note: Antiochus IX was captured and killed (Josephus) or killed himself (Eusebius). Site unknown.

name: Cilicia (Antiochus X v Seleucus VI)
note: Antiochus X defeated Seleucus VI, who fled to Mopsuestia and died there; the battlefield is not stated.

name: Orontes
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Antiochus X v Antiochus XI)
sources: Jos. AJ 13.369; Euseb. Chron. (Porphyry FGrH 260 F32)
note: Antiochus XI drowned in the Orontes while fleeing. Eusebius has Philip I fight alongside him; Josephus only Antiochus XI.

name: Antiochus X v Parthians
place: unknown (in support of Laodice, queen of the 'Gileadites/Sameni')
note: Very uncertain: only Josephus reports that Antiochus X fell fighting the Parthians as an ally of Queen Laodice; Appian and Eusebius give other ends. Laodice's people and the site are unidentified (Samosata/Commagene has been suggested, which would place it in Turkey); placed generically on the Syrian Euphrates.

name: Amnias
note: Pontic scythed chariots and cavalry routed Nicomedes' much larger army.

name: Mount Scorobas
place: Mount Scorobas, on the Bithynian–Pontic frontier
note: Cavalry clash: 100 Sarmatian horse of Mithridates defeated 800 Bithynian cavalry. Small; included because standard works list it as a battle.

name: Protopachium
note: Aquillius lost about 10,000 men; the Romans abandoned Bithynia.

name: Rhodes
sources: App. Mith. 24–26; Memnon 22.8; Diod. 37.28; Val. Max. 5.2.ext.2
note: Naval fighting during Mithridates' siege of Rhodes: a fleet action off the harbour in which Mithridates' own ship was rammed by an allied Chian vessel, and a Rhodian attack on storm-scattered Pontic ships (about 400 captured). The land assaults (siege) are not counted.

name: Delos
note: Borderline: a night attack by the Roman Orbius on the carelessly encamped expedition sent by Aristion's (pro-Mithridatic) Athens; 600 killed, 400 captured.

name: Shechem
war: Judean civil war / Demetrius III's invasion
note: Demetrius was invited by Jannaeus' Jewish opponents; all of Jannaeus' Greek mercenaries fell. Demetrius withdrew soon after when many Jews returned to Jannaeus.

name: Off Egypt (Tyrrhus v Ptolemy X)
war: Ptolemaic civil war (expulsion of Ptolemy X)
place: unknown, presumably off the Egyptian coast
note: After his expulsion from Alexandria Ptolemy X returned with a force and was beaten at sea by Tyrrhus, then fled to Myra in Lycia. Site unknown.

name: Cyprus (Chaereas v Ptolemy X)
war: Ptolemaic civil war (expulsion of Ptolemy X)
note: Ptolemy X, with forces raised at Myra, invaded Cyprus and fell in a naval action against Chaereas (Smith's reading of Porphyry); some modern accounts treat it as a land fight on Cyprus.

name: Sciathos
note: Small naval action: Sura sank a large ship and a hemiolia of Metrophanes' squadron, then stormed Sciathos. Site not stated.

name: Chaeronea
note: Three days of fighting, indecisive per Appian (Plutarch implies Sura had the better); Sura withdrew when Spartan and Achaean forces joined Archelaus.

name: Piraeus (sortie)
note: Sortie battle during the siege: Archelaus led his whole army out; after long doubtful fighting the Romans killed about 2,000 and drove the rest inside. Other sorties were smaller.

name: Chalcis
note: Sulla's legate Minucius defeated Neoptolemus, killing 1,500 and capturing more.

name: Beroea
war: Seleucid dynastic wars (Philip I v Demetrius III)
commanders_a: Mithridates Sinaces (Parthian), Aziz/Zizon (Arab phylarch), Straton tyrant of Beroea
note: Borderline (blockade of a field army): Demetrius, besieging his brother Philip I in Beroea, was himself surrounded in his camp by the Parthian and Arab relief forces called in by Straton, shot at and forced by thirst to surrender; sent to Mithridates II. Philip I's faction listed as ally.

name: Orchomenus
place: plain near Orchomenus by the Copaic marshes
sources: Plut. Sulla 20–21; App. Mith. 49–50; Frontin. Str. 2.8.12
note: Fought over two days (field battle, then storming of the Pontic camp); counted as one battle.

name: Lectum
note: Lucullus' fleet, largely of Rhodian and other allied ships, defeated a royal squadron; no details.

name: Tenedos
commanders_a: L. Licinius Lucullus, Damagoras of Rhodes
note: Lucullus fought from a Rhodian ship commanded by Damagoras.

name: Rhyndacus
commanders_b: Mithridates (son of Mithridates VI), Taxiles, Diophantus, Menander
note: Also called the battle of Miletopolis: a cavalry victory followed by a dawn attack across the river on the Pontic camp.

name: Cana
place: south or south-west of the Dead Sea; army perished at 'Cana' (Motho?)
sources: Jos. AJ 13.387–391, BJ 1.99–102; Steph. Byz. s.v. Motho (Uranius)
note: 10,000 Arab horsemen fell on Antiochus' army; the king was killed and the survivors starved at Cana. Site unknown; Nabataean king usually taken as Obodas I (deified afterwards), Josephus names Aretas as the beneficiary.

name: Halys
note: Appian: Murena routed and driven back into Phrygia; Memnon calls the battle evenly balanced.

name: Chalcedon
commanders_b: M. Aurelius Cotta, P. Rutilius Nudus
sources: App. Mith. 71; Memnon 27.7–8; Plut. Luc. 8; Sall. Hist. 3; Oros. 6.2.13
note: Pontic Bastarnae routed the Roman army outside the city (Memnon: 5,300 Roman dead on land). Fought the same day as the harbour battle.

name: Chalcedon (sea)
note: The Pontic fleet broke the harbour chain, burned 4 Roman ships and towed off 60 (Memnon: about 8,000 Roman losses at sea).

name: Rhyndacus
place: crossing of the river Rhyndacus, during the siege of Cyzicus
sources: Plut. Luc. 11.3–6; App. Mith. 75; Memnon 28; Oros. 6.2.15
note: Lucullus caught Mithridates' cavalry and baggage train sent away from the Cyzicus siege; 15,000 men and 6,000 horses captured.

name: Granicus
place: crossings of the Aesepus and Granicus, Mysia
sources: Plut. Luc. 11.8; App. Mith. 76; Memnon 28.4; Oros. 6.2.20
note: Destruction of the Pontic army retreating from Cyzicus at the river crossings (some 20,000 killed); partly a pursuit rather than a pitched battle.

name: Phrygia (Deiotarus v Eumachus)
note: The Galatian tetrarch Deiotarus (a Roman ally) defeated and drove out Mithridates' general Eumachus; possibly several engagements.

name: Tenedos
place: between Tenedos and the Achaean harbour, Troad
note: Lucullus captured 13 Pontic quinqueremes; Isidorus killed.

name: Lemnos
place: islet of Neae, between Lemnos and Scyros
sources: Plut. Luc. 12.3–5; App. Mith. 77; Memnon 29, 33.1; Cic. Leg. Man. 21; Oros. 6.2.21–22
note: Lucullus landed troops behind the beached Pontic squadron and destroyed it (32 ships); the Sertorian M. Marius was captured and executed.

name: Cabira
commanders_a: L. Licinius Lucullus, M. Fabius Hadrianus, Sornatius
sources: Plut. Luc. 15–17; App. Mith. 79–82; Memnon 29.8–30.1; Sall. Hist. 4
note: Campaign of several actions: early Pontic cavalry successes, then the destruction of the cavalry sent against Lucullus' supply convoys, followed by panic and collapse of Mithridates' army. Counted as one battle.

name: Tenedos
note: Triarius with 70 triremes destroyed the Pontic squadron (just under 80 ships) returning from Crete and Spain. Known only from Memnon.

name: Crete (Antonius' defeat)
sources: Flor. 1.42.1–3; Diod. 40.1; Livy Per. 97; App. Sic. 6; Sall. Hist. 3
note: Cretan cities led by Cydonia and Knossos captured much of Antonius' fleet and hanged prisoners from the rigging; exact site unknown.

name: Heraclea Pontica
place: approach to the harbour of Heraclea Pontica
note: Triarius' 43 ships (20 of them Rhodian) defeated the 30-ship Heracleote fleet during the siege of the city (Heraclea was allied to Mithridates; siege not counted).

name: Sinope
note: Ships of the Sinope garrison defeated Censorinus' 15 triremes escorting grain transports and seized the transports, during Lucullus' siege of Sinope.

name: Cydonia
sources: App. Sic. 6.5; Livy Per. 98; Phlegon fr. 12.12
note: Metellus defeated the Cretan army (Lasthenes of Knossos, Panares of Cydonia), then besieged Cydonia, Knossos and other cities (sieges not counted).

name: Arsanias
place: river Arsanias (Murat), Armenia, on Lucullus' march to Artaxata
sources: Plut. Luc. 31.4–8; App. Mith. 87; Dio 36.4–5; Sall. Hist. 4
note: Included because Mithridates was co-commander (Appian says Tigranes gave him the command; Plutarch has him leading a large cavalry force and fleeing first). Also called the battle of Artaxata; site disputed.

name: Pontus (Fabius' defeat)
sources: App. Mith. 88; Dio 36.9.2–5; Plut. Luc. 35.1; Sall. Hist. 5
note: Returning to Pontus, Mithridates defeated Lucullus' legate Fabius, who was saved only when Mithridates was wounded.

name: Comana
note: Known only from Dio; identification of Comana uncertain.

name: Zela
note: About 7,000 Romans killed, including 24 tribunes and 150 centurions.

name: Lycus
place: by the river Lycus, near later Nicopolis, Lesser Armenia
sources: Plut. Pomp. 32; App. Mith. 99–100; Dio 36.48–49; Oros. 6.4.3–5
note: Pompey's night attack on Mithridates' army in a defile; Pompey founded Nicopolis on the site. Also called the battle of Nicopolis or Dasteira.

name: Pelusium
place: eastern Delta, on the march from Pelusium
note: Roman army restoring Ptolemy XII against the regime of Berenice IV; after Pelusium was taken (Antony's cavalry), Gabinius defeated the Egyptians the same day. Hyrcanus/Antipater's Judaeans gave support.

name: Nile
place: on and beside the Nile in the Delta (site unknown)
note: Combined land and river battle in which Archelaus was killed; Ptolemy XII restored.

name: Massalia
place: off Massalia, near the island opposite the city
note: Massaliote fleet of 17 warships (with Domitius' Pompeian crews) defeated by Brutus; 9 ships lost.

name: Tauroeis
note: Second Massaliote fleet, joined by Nasidius' 16 Pompeian ships (which fled without fighting), defeated with 9 ships lost. The city later capitulated (siege not counted).

name: Alexandria (harbour)
note: Fight for the Egyptian fleet in the harbour; Caesar burned the ships (fire said to have reached the Library) and occupied the Pharos tower. Egypt's side was the army of Ptolemy XIII (later Arsinoe IV and Ganymedes), opposed to Cleopatra VII.

name: Nicopolis
note: Pharnaces II, king of the Cimmerian Bosporus, fighting to recover his father's Pontic kingdom (counted as Pontus). Two of Calvinus' four legions were Deiotarus' Galatians; Ariobarzanes III of Cappadocia sent cavalry.

name: Chersonesus
note: Egyptian ships attacked Caesar's fleet while it covered the arrival of the 37th legion; Euphranor's Rhodian ships bore the brunt; one quadrireme captured and another sunk.

name: Alexandria (sea)
place: off Alexandria, by the shoals west of Pharos
note: Caesar's 34 ships (9 Rhodian, led by Euphranor) defeated the fleet Ganymedes had rebuilt.

name: Pharos
place: island and town of Pharos, Alexandria
note: Amphibious assault: Caesar captured the Pharos island town from its defenders.

name: Heptastadion
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 19–21; Plut. Caes. 49; Suet. Caes. 64; Dio 42.40
note: Fight for the mole the day after Pharos, with Egyptian ships joining in; Caesar's men were routed (c. 400 legionaries and many sailors lost) and Caesar escaped by swimming.

name: Canopus
note: Egyptian attempt to intercept supply convoys was repulsed, but Euphranor, pursuing too far, was surrounded and killed; arguably indecisive.

name: Delta (Jews' Camp)
place: Nile Delta, at the place called the Camp of the Jews
note: Caesar's relief army under Mithridates of Pergamon (Syrian, Cilician, Nabataean and Ituraean contingents, 3,000 Jews under Antipater) defeated the Egyptian force sent against it after the capture of Pelusium; Josephus credits Antipater with saving the day. Identified with Tell el-Yahudiya (approx.).

name: Nile
date: 47 BCE (27 March Roman calendar; c. January 47 Julian)
place: near a Nile tributary, western Delta
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 28–31; Livy Per. 112; Joseph. AJ 14.136; Dio 42.43; Oros. 6.16
note: Ptolemy XIII drowned in the flight; Cleopatra VII restored with Ptolemy XIV.

name: Zela
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 72–77; Plut. Caes. 50; Suet. Caes. 35, 37; App. BC 2.91, Mith. 120; Dio 42.47
note: 'Veni, vidi, vici.' Pharnaces II (king of the Bosporus) counted as Pontus.

name: Bosporus (Pharnaces v Asander)
note: After Zela, Pharnaces recovered Theodosia and Panticapaeum but was killed fighting his rebel governor Asander.

name: Bosporus (Mithridates of Pergamon v Asander)
note: Mithridates of Pergamon, made king of the Bosporus by Caesar, was 'overthrown' by Asander and died; that it was a pitched battle is probable but not explicit.

name: Myndus
note: 33 Rhodian ships surrounded by Cassius' larger and heavier fleet; 3 captured and 2 sunk.

name: Rhodes
note: Small engagement: the Rhodians sailed out against Cassius' 80 ships from Loryma, lost two more ships and were shut in; the city then fell (siege not counted).

name: Actium
war: War of Actium (Octavian v Antony and Cleopatra)
place: mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, off Actium
note: War formally declared on Cleopatra; Antony's Roman fleet and legions fought with her Egyptian squadron (also a Roman civil war, so Rome appears on both sides). Client kings with Antony included Archelaus of Cappadocia and Mithridates of Commagene; Polemon of Pontus sent troops.

name: Paraetonium
war: War of Actium (Octavian v Antony and Cleopatra)
note: Antony's attack on Gallus' army from Cyrenaica failed: his land assault was repulsed and his ships were trapped by chains in the harbour and destroyed.

name: Alexandria (Hippodrome)
war: War of Actium (Octavian v Antony and Cleopatra)
place: near the Hippodrome, east of Alexandria
note: Antony's cavalry routed Octavian's tired vanguard cavalry and pursued it to its camp.

name: Alexandria
war: War of Actium (Octavian v Antony and Cleopatra)
note: Antony's combined land and sea attack collapsed when his fleet and cavalry went over to Octavian; his infantry was defeated. End of the Ptolemaic kingdom (Antony and Cleopatra's suicides followed).

name: Bosporus (Polemon I v the Bosporans)
note: Agrippa sent Polemon against the usurper Scribonius; the Bosporans had already killed Scribonius but resisted Polemon, fearing he would be made their king. Polemon fought and defeated them, but they submitted only when Agrippa came to Sinope; Polemon then married Dynamis and ruled the Bosporus. Falls after batch 08's end (30 BCE) but inside the brief's range (to c. 10 CE). Polemon's later death at the hands of the Aspurgiani (c. 8 BCE, Strabo 11.2.11, 12.3.29) was a capture after a failed surprise attack, not a recorded battle, so it is not added. Polemon was a Roman client king acting for Agrippa.
